item.title: Social media tributes pour in for former Bears head coach Mike Ditka, who passed away at 86
item.description: The Hall of Famer had become a beloved icon thanks to his mustache and the memorable impressions of him, which added humor to his normally stoic demeanor.
item.content:encoded:
Jarrett Payton, son of former Chicago Bears running back Walter Payton, posted that the Ditka family announced Mike Ditka's death Friday morning. He was 86 years old.

It’s with a heavy heart that I’m sharing the Ditka family has announced the passing of Mike Ditka this morning.
Da Coach. Hall of Famer. The heartbeat of the ’85 Bears and a Super Bowl champion. Chicago won’t be the same.
Prayers to Diana and the family.
RIP, Coach. 🐻⬇️

Here’s… pic.twitter.com/NUDfwsjaNH

— Jarrett Payton (@paytonsun) October 9, 2026

Ditka played tight end in the NFL from 1961 to 1972, spending his first six years in Chicago. Over his 12-year career, he caught 427 passes for 5,812 yards and 43 touchdowns, earning 5 Pro Bowl selections.

He returned to the Windy City as head coach in 1982 and coached the Bears for 11 seasons.

The '85 Bears are known as one of the best defenses in NFL history. Ditka led them to a 15-1 record and a Super Bowl XX win over the New England Patriots. It remains the franchise's only Super Bowl win.

Ditka finished his coaching career with a 121-95 record and one Super Bowl title. He was the first tight end inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame, enshrined in the Class of 1988.

Tributes to Ditka and his impact on the NFL and football poured in on social media.

The NFL is deeply saddened by the passing of Hall of Fame coach and tight end, Mike Ditka.

Our thoughts are with his family and loved ones. ❤️ pic.twitter.com/H9cMGPc8ln

— NFL (@NFL) October 9, 2026

Ditka attended the University of Pittsburgh from 1958 to 1960. His alma mater paid tribute to their former Panther.

A True Pitt Man.

Rest In Peace, Mike Ditka. pic.twitter.com/wAdMlf5dvZ

— Pitt Football (@Pitt_FB) October 9, 2026

Ozzie Guillen paid tribute to Ditka, from one from head coach of a Chicago sports team to another.

Coach, man, we had some great times, laughs, and memories over the years. Always admired your style. Thank you for the talks, advice, and friendship.
Chicago lost a legend Rest easy, Coach. pic.twitter.com/J5x4BkyuLc

— Ozzie Guillen (@OzzieGuillen) October 9, 2026

While Ditka is known for his tenure as the head coach of the Bears, he ended his coaching career with the New Orleans Saints. He went 15-33 over three seasons with the team from 1997 to 1999.

The New Orleans Saints organization mourns the passing of NFL icon Mike Ditka, who passed away today at the age of 86.

The New Orleans Saints organization mourns the passing of NFL icon Mike Ditka, who passed away today at the age of 86. We extend our deepest condolences to the… pic.twitter.com/EhbG6TuLN2

— New Orleans Saints (@Saints) October 9, 2026

Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka, whose toughness and leadership helped define an era of professional football, passed away at the age of 86, his family announced Friday. A member of the Hall's Class of 1988, Ditka's legacy as a player, coach and football icon will endure… pic.twitter.com/1eHsn554d5

— Pro Football Hall of Fame (@ProFootballHOF) October 9, 2026

Green Bay Packers head coach offered condolences during his Friday press conference. The Packers will face the Bears at Lambeau Field on Sunday in the latest iteration of their historic rivalry.

Matt LaFleur offers his condolences for the late Mike Ditka ahead of Packers-Bears on Sunday pic.twitter.com/m4Iov8VxXY

— Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) October 9, 2026

Lions head coach Dan Campbell learned of Ditka’s passing during his press conference. He instantly started regaling the media with a story about Ditka.

#Lions HC Dan Campbell learned of Mike Ditka’s passing during his press conference and gave a raw, immediate reaction + sharing a personal story. 🙏 https://t.co/Utwe9rCh8lpic.twitter.com/07cl1WVUob

— Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 9, 2026

Ditka was known for his seriousness on the field and his rants. The head coach pushed that to the side in 2005 as he starred alongside Will Ferrell in “Kicking and Screaming” where the pair were the head coach and assistant coach of a youth soccer team.

BREAKING: Bears legend Mike Ditka has passed away at 86 years old. That means two legends who share this scene together from Kicking & Screaming, Robert Duvall & Mike Ditka, have both passed away in 2026. Ditka - whether you liked him or not - was undeniably charismatic. It shows… pic.twitter.com/kCvBDOAtOf

— Cinema Tweets (@CinemaTweets1) October 9, 2026

I am so incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Mike Ditka. His playing & coaching prowess is well documented. A legit 🐐. But more importantly...he was kind, supportive and funny. When I first got to ESPN there were definitely ex NFL stars (and others!) that looked at the… pic.twitter.com/3PWIB4U3Wu

— Matthew Berry (@MatthewBerryTMR) October 9, 2026

Ditka became the first tight end ever inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He is also the only player ever to have at least 100 receptions as a player, 100 wins as a head coach, and a Super Bowl win as both player and coach.

The only man in NFL history with 100+ career catches and a Super Bowl win as a player, then 100+ wins and a Super Bowl title as a coach. RIP Mike Ditka 🐻#DaBearshttps://t.co/uREBTzpJRS

item.title: Who’s to blame for the Las Vegas Raiders’ woeful rushing attack?
item.description: The Las Vegas Raiders ran the ball 26 times for 72 yards and no touchdowns against the Kansas City Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
The Las Vegas Raiders didn’t run the ball efficiently against the Kansas City Chiefs. Before we dive into what they did wrong, credit must be given where credit is due. Peter Woods, Felix Anudike-Uzomah, Chris Jones and Khyiris Tonga did a helluva job giving the Raiders’ offensive line absolute fits in their run defense.

Throughout the entire game, the Chiefs defensive line initiated contact and brought the fight to the Raiders’ run blockers. Woods is a large man who plays angry; moving him continuously was a problem, even with duos (double teams). In fact, the Chiefs’ defensive line did well at defeating double teams and combo blocks. When they weren’t outright defeating those blocks, they disrupted pathways for Raiders linemen to climb to the second level and block linebackers.

On one particular play, Chris Jones maintained 2-gap integrity by keeping outside leverage, temporarily opening the inside gap before defeating Caleb Rogers’ blocking attempt and forcing Mike Washington Jr. back toward his help. What looked like a play where the designed hole was open and a cutback lane formed ended up being a run stuff for the defense.

Spencer Burford has been a factor in the run game; when he succeeds, the run game is a beautiful thing to watch. However, when he is getting pancaked by a defensive tackle on the line of scrimmage, there is no hope. Burford got sat on his butt so fast by the man he was trying to block that it took a great reaction by Washington to avoid him and bounce the run outside to gain positive yards.

Klint Kubiak’s scheme could use some tweaks

When Kubiak told reporters he needs to scheme the run game better, he was spot on. Despite utilizing 12/13 personnel the most in the league, he’s not receiving the results he seeks. Part of it is actually the lack of creativity, surprising considering Kubiak’s chalkboard mastery of the passing attack. More often than not, the offensive player going in motion is leading the defense directly to the ball.

Lacking any consistent type of misdirection may work when you have a numbers advantage on the play side, or superior size and push upfront from the offensive line. But when enough weeks of film are available, tendencies begin to display themselves as they are formed. Like running inside zone on first downs, or running to the edges on second downs when not passing. There haven’t been many, if any, endarounds, fly sweeps, or counter plays. Not a lot of draws, nor many running back screens.

It was definitely something Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo picked up on when studying film. How do we know this? The Chiefs defense made a concentrated effort to sell out against the run game. Whenever a receiver or tight end went in motion, the linebackers shifted over as soon as the offensive player crossed behind the center. A safety rolled into the box to overload a side of the line of scrimmage by creating a numbers advantage.

Figuring out a way to be less obvious with the run game is vital to getting it going again. The Raiders offensive line isn’t bad, and according to nearly every analytics site out there, they are a top-ten unit. But two things can be equally true: the run-block win rate can be ranked high, but when the defense brings extra heat, the unblocked defender is killing the effectiveness of the run game.

Not getting a push

Without being privileged to sit inside the offensive line room, it’s hard to speak on what exactly the blocking scheme is. Breaking down film, we have to slow it down to about 1/2 speed or lower to watch the line go through their assignments. Free agent Center, Tyler Linderbaum is the best at engaging in a duo block and then climbing to the second level. From time to time, Burford will pull and lead the running back through the hole.

No push is most noticeable in short-yardage-to-go situations. The tush push run by Connor Heyward has been executed flawlessly; however, counting on the run from longer than three yards will make you hang your head. The Raiders run into the highest percentage of stacked boxes and consequently running back Ashton Jeanty has been hit in the backfield at an alarming rate.

Offensive linemen getting pushed into the backfield disrupts the scheme as a whole, not just the running back. In the Chiefs game alone, there were quite a few times when pulling and motioning blockers were not able to get to their assignments because they were disrupted by a fellow lineman getting blown up and pushed into their path.

Lacking vision, no trust and not enough burst

Any NFL running back worth a salt would admonish being compared to “T-rich,” Trent Richardson, who was ‘T-rash” when it came to field vision. Speed in the NFL is at a completely different level; players simply move faster than most can anticipate. Holes open and close in a fraction of a second, but that is on the running back to be able to see them, make quick decisions to change course and burst through them.

Which brings us to a lack of trust in the blocking. Either the running backs don’t see the hole or don’t think they can make it through in time. Whatever the case, some holes aren’t being run through. This is frustrating to watch and a shame. Raiders’ outside runs are being negatively impacted by runners looking for cutbacks instead of focusing on hitting holes. Not being able to burst through open gaps and creases is exactly why the running game has been struggling.

item.title: The Rams have mismanaged this special teams role for longer than a year
item.description: Eagle’s Britain Covey reminded Rams how they have botched punt returner role for a long time
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams had a front row seat last weekend to watch one of the NFL’s best punt return men. Britain Covey playing well for the Philadelphia Eagles despite spending last training camp with the Rams.

Covey serves as a reminder of how—after all this time—LA still does not prioritize special teams. The Rams chose Xavier Smith over Covey out of training camp last year. That ended with Smith fumbling a punt return in the NFC Championship game.

LA is struggling on special teams. It’s an issue that spans broader than a single bad decision surrounding which punt returner to keep. The Rams have made many poor special teams missteps. Covey is simply a symbol of the dysfunction.

How did the Rams let Covey walk?

Xavier Smith returned 16 punts over the 2024 season for 149 yards (9.3 average). He was kept out of the end zone and broke only a single return longer than 20 yards. Smith had the sixth-most fair catches that year with 20.

Meanwhile Covey lost the punt return job in Philadelphia to then-rookie Cooper DeJean. He became expendable. The Rams brought him in to compete with Smith.

But there truly was no preseason or camp competition. Smith was sidelined as LA’s returner in the preseason. Instead, Covey, Drake Stoops, and Brennan Presley were the only players to field punts in the 2025 exhibition games. Covey wasn’t going to make the roster as a pure receiver. He was released and found his way back to Philadelphia.

Over the 2025 regular season Covey returned 11 punts for 124 yards (11.3 average) with one broken off for longer than 20 yards. Smith was consistent with his 2024 production on a per return basis. He averaged 9.3 yards despite a volume increase from 16 to 27 returns. Smith earned three returns longer than 20 yards with a long of 31.

The Rams still don’t have a returner

Last Sunday in a head-to-head matchup, Covey returned three punts for 59 yards (19.7 average) with a long of 41. Smith was cut leading up to the game and replaced by Alex Bachman, who had three opportunities and managed a measly average of just 7.5 yards.

On the season Covey ranks eighth in punt return average across the NFL. He already has two returns longer than 20 yards. The Rams are getting bottom of the league production from their specialists.

And that matters. Poor starting field position increases the degree of difficulty for Matthew Stafford and the offense, which can help explain why one of the best units in the NFL from a year ago is suddenly buck average.

Smith clearly wasn’t good enough. Bachman has somehow been worse.

The decision to keep Smith over Covey in 2025 was egregiously bad. The Rams still have not course corrected.

It’s one step in a long line of poor special teams management. Britain Covey reminded LA last weekend how far they have fallen in the third phase.

item.title: Flashback Friday: The last time the Chiefs were undefeated at the bye
item.description: How similar is Kansas City’s hot start to the season when compared to the 2024 campaign?
item.content:encoded:
This weekend, the Kansas City Chiefs and the Carolina Panthers will have an off-day while the rest of the NFL plays Week 6. It’s the first week the league schedule includes a bye.

Two years ago, the Chiefs were in a similar position: after a Week 5 win over the New Orleans Saints on “Monday Night Football,” Kansas City entered an early bye week undefeated (5-0) with crucial conference wins over the Baltimore Ravens and Cincinnati Bengals as well as a road victory against the Los Angeles Chargers.

In that road win over the Chargers, the Chiefs suffered a crucial injury to the receiving corps: second-year wideout Rashee Rice tore his ACL while trying to make a tackle after an interception.

The start of the 2024 season sounds eerily similar to this year’s. The offense will need to move forward without one of its top receivers, Tyquan Thornton, but it has the benefit of a lead in the standings, with wins over the Denver Broncos and Las Vegas Raiders.

In 2024, the Chiefs continued the hot streak into Week 11: Kansas City won four straight games after the Week 6 bye before falling to the Buffalo Bills on the road. That featured a road trip to face a contending NFC West team (the San Francisco 49ers) and a division rival (the Raiders).

Can the 2026 Chiefs stay undefeated through this year’s road trip to Buffalo? It would also require surviving a West Coast trip, this time against the Seattle Seahawks and Broncos.

The biggest difference between this season’s team and the squad that was attempting to finish off a three-peat is the offense. In the first five games of 2024, the Chiefs’ highest-scoring output was 27 points. Through Week 5, the season-high rushing total was 149, in a game where starting running back Isiah Pacheco broke a bone in his leg.

This year, the Chiefs have scored 30 or more points in three of their four games, and running back Kenneth Walker has surpassed 148 rushing yards twice on his own.

The offense will need to keep finding ways to score despite the significant injury. In 2024, that meant trading for All-Pro wide receiver DeAndre Hopkins. He scored two touchdowns in his second game in Kansas City, but he didn’t make a big-time impact on the field through the team’s AFC championship run that year.

General manager Brett Veach made that move when the team was 6-0. He doesn’t like wasting opportunities to win Super Bowls when quarterback Patrick Mahomes is at the helm. The receiver position could use a similar boost, but it remains to be seen whether the younger pass catchers will step up in Thornton’s place.

Regardless, this year’s Chiefs need to finish stronger than the 2024 team did. The wheels fell off against the Philadelphia Eagles in Super Bowl LIX, and a major factor was an injury at left tackle. This year, the team has made it work with rookie Kahlil Benson on the left side, but the health of last year’s first-round pick, Josh Simmons, could be key to avoiding a disappointing end to the season in Kansas City.

item.title: 15 meetings, plenty of memories: A look back at Bills-Rams history
item.description: From Frank Reich's Monday night heroics to Josh Allen's six-TD loss, Bills-Rams history has delivered plenty of drama
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams don’t have the kind of rivalry that comes from playing twice a season, but their occasional meetings have produced some pretty memorable moments. There have been last-second touchdowns, Hall of Fame milestones, a Super Bowl celebration spoiled, and a six-touchdown performance that somehow wasn’t enough to win. 

The two franchises have met 15 times since 1970, with Buffalo holding a 9–6 advantage. The Bills have won five of the last six, although the Rams claimed the most recent meeting in a game that might still give Buffalo fans a headache. 

With the Bills headed to Los Angeles for Monday Night Football, it’s time to open the Time Capsule and revisit some of the history between these two teams. 

____________________________________________________________________________

The early years: Los Angeles gets the better of Buffalo 

The Bills and Rams first crossed paths on September 27, 1970, during the NFL’s first season following the AFL-NFL merger. Buffalo had spent the previous decade in the AFL, winning back-to-back championships in 1964 and 1965, while Los Angeles had been part of the NFL since 1937. 

The Rams weren’t especially welcoming. They traveled to Buffalo and handed the Bills a 19–0 shutout, beginning a stretch in which Los Angeles won three of the first four meetings between the franchises. 

Buffalo’s first win didn’t come until December 7, 1980, when the Bills earned a 10–7 win at home. It was hardly an offensive showcase, but it finally put Buffalo in the win column against a team that had reached the Super Bowl the previous season. 

The Rams responded with a 41–17 victory in 1983, leaving Buffalo trailing the series 3–1. It would be another six years before the two teams met again, and by then the Bills were building a roster that would eventually lead them to four consecutive Super Bowls. 

____________________________________________________________________________

The Super Bowl years: Reich, Thomas, and a little Monday night magic 

The Rams had gotten the better of Buffalo through the first four meetings, but that changed in 1989. The Bills would win the next three matchups, including a Monday night thriller and a blowout that put a future Hall of Famer into the NFL record books. 

On October 16, 1989, an undefeated Rams team arrived at Rich Stadium for Monday Night Football. Jim Kelly was sidelined with a shoulder injury, leaving backup Frank Reich to make his first NFL start. 

For most of the evening, Reich did enough to keep Buffalo competitive. A fourth-quarter touchdown pass to Thurman Thomas gave the Bills a 16–13 lead, and when Buffalo recovered possession late in the game, it appeared the outcome was settled. 

Then Thomas fumbled. 

Los Angeles recovered, and Jim Everett connected with Flipper Anderson for a 78-yard touchdown. Suddenly, the Rams led 20–16 with just 1:22 remaining. 

Reich, who had never started an NFL game before that evening, responded by completing seven consecutive passes. The final one went eight yards to Andre Reed for the winning touchdown with 16 seconds left on the clock. Buffalo won 23–20, handing Los Angeles its first defeat of the season. 

It wasn’t the comeback that would eventually make Reich famous, but it was an early demonstration of what the Bills had waiting behind Kelly on the depth chart. 

Three years later, the Rams returned to Buffalo for the 1992 season opener. This time, there would be no need for a dramatic finish. 

The Bills rolled to a 40–7 win, the largest margin in the history of the series. Thomas scored four touchdowns, three on the ground and one through the air, while Buffalo’s defense intercepted Rams quarterback Jim Everett four times. 

But the afternoon wasn’t entirely about the scoreboard. 

Veteran receiver James Lofton, already one of the NFL’s most accomplished pass catchers, surpassed Steve Largent to become the league’s all-time leader in career receiving yards that day. Lofton finished the afternoon with six catches for 56 yards, adding an NFL record to a game that also marked the beginning of Buffalo’s third consecutive Super Bowl run. 

The Bills would add another win over the Rams in 1995, winning 45–27 in the franchises’ first meeting after the Rams relocated to St. Louis. 

____________________________________________________________________________

The St. Louis years: Buffalo maintains the upper hand 

The Rams moved to St. Louis in 1995, where they would eventually become the Greatest Show on Turf, win a Super Bowl with Kurt Warner, and spend 21 seasons before returning to Los Angeles. 

Interestingly, the Bills never faced that championship team. 

The franchises met five times while the Rams called St. Louis home, with Buffalo winning three of those matchups. The Bills took the first meeting in 1995 with a 45–27 win, but the Rams squeaked out a 34–33 victory in 1998. Buffalo responded with wins in 2004 and 2008 before St. Louis got the last word in 2012, winning 15–12 in what would be the teams’ final meeting before the Rams returned to Los Angeles. 

____________________________________________________________________________

The Josh Allen era: Big wins, bigger numbers, and one painful loss 

By the time the Bills and Rams met again in September 2020, Buffalo had a new franchise quarterback and was beginning to establish itself as an AFC contender. 

The first meeting of the Allen era almost became a disaster. 

Buffalo built a 28–3 lead in the third quarter at Bills Stadium, only to watch Jared Goff and the Rams score 29 unanswered points. Los Angeles led 32–28 with less than five minutes remaining, leaving Allen to rescue a game that he had seemed to have had comfortably in hand. 

The quarterback directed a 75-yard touchdown drive, aided by a controversial fourth-down pass interference call, and found Tyler Kroft in the end zone with 15 seconds remaining. Buffalo escaped with a 35–32 victory and a 3–0 start to the season. 

Two years later, the Bills returned to face the Rams under considerably brighter lights. 

Los Angeles was coming off its victory in Super Bowl LVI, and the NFL had selected Buffalo as the opponent for the league’s traditional Thursday night season opener. The Rams were raising a championship banner at SoFi Stadium, but the Bills had no intention of contributing to the celebration. 

The teams went into halftime tied at 10, despite Buffalo turning the ball over three times in the first two quarters. The second half was a completely different game. 

Allen threw three touchdown passes and added another score on the ground, while the Buffalo defense intercepted Matthew Stafford three times and sacked him seven times. The Bills scored 21 unanswered second-half points and left Los Angeles with a convincing 31–10 victory. 

The Bills returned to Los Angeles two years later, and Allen had an even bigger game. Unfortunately for Buffalo, the Rams had a pretty good day, too. 

On December 8, 2024, the Bills returned to SoFi Stadium riding a seven-game winning streak. Allen was in the middle of what would become his first NFL MVP season, and he delivered one of the most remarkable individual performances in league history. 

He threw for 342 yards and three touchdowns. He rushed for 82 yards and three more scores. In doing so, he became the first player in NFL history to throw three touchdown passes and rush for three touchdowns in the same game. 

Six touchdowns. No turnovers. And a loss. 

Stafford threw for 320 yards and two touchdowns, while Puka Nacua caught 12 passes for 162 yards and scored twice, once receiving and once rushing. The Rams built a 38–21 lead entering the fourth quarter, forcing Buffalo into another desperate comeback attempt. 

Allen nearly pulled it off. His third rushing touchdown brought the Bills within two points in the final minute, but Los Angeles recovered the ensuing onside kick and held on for the 44–42 win. 

The teams combined for 86 points and more than 900 yards of offense. Buffalo scored more points than any losing team in franchise history. 

____________________________________________________________________________

Another Monday night chapter awaits 

That 44–42 loss was the last time the Bills and Rams shared a field. Now, nearly two years later, Buffalo is headed back to SoFi Stadium for another prime-time matchup, and Allen will have another chance to get the better of Matthew Stafford. 

There’s also a little more hardware between the two quarterbacks this time around. Allen won NFL MVP honors for the 2024 season, and Stafford followed him with the award in 2025. 

The Bills and Rams have never met in the postseason, but who’s to say a Super Bowl matchup isn’t somewhere in their future? For now, we’ll settle for another Monday night game. Hopefully, this one ends with the Bills on the right side of the scoreboard, no matter how many touchdowns Allen scores.

item.title: Why the Seahawks signing Terrion Arnold for one year was never about 2026
item.description: Arnold signed a one-year contract with Seattle, but because of the CBA the team can keep him around through at least 2027 should they so desire.
item.content:encoded:
Through the first four weeks of the season the Seattle Seahawks have battled a number of injuries in the secondary, and many fans had hoped that the recent hearing in the ongoing legal case of Terrion Arnold might shed some light on when Arnold might be able to contribute.

Obviously, no such light was shed, and with the next court date for Arnold scheduled for December 15, it seems likely that no update is coming soon. This has some fans inquiring as to why the Seahawks even bothered to sign Arnold to a one-year contract, because at the present the likelihood of any on-field contributions during the 2026 season seem minimal.

Specifically, the December 15 court date comes just ahead of Week 15, so even if a trial date is set at that hearing, it seems almost impossible for any conclusion to the matter to come before the end of the season, meaning Arnold will remain on the Commissioner’s Exempt List, will continue to get paid and his current contract will expire without ever having set foot on the field for Seattle.

With that being the case, some have started to ask what the point is for Seattle to keep Arnold on the roster and continue to pay him $59,722 each week to not practice and not play, when there seems very little possibility for him to contribute in 2026.

The answer to that question requires a deep dive into the collective bargaining agreement to understand that Seattle signing Arnold to a one-year contract was likely never about 2026, and was more so about 2027 and beyond.

That, of course, seems paradoxical because the one year contract Arnold signed only covers 2026, so he’s not under contract for 2027, and therefore to understand the machination behind why, it’s necessary to turn to some light reading in the form of the collective bargaining agreement.

To jump right to the point, it is Article 8, Section 1(a) that is relevant to Arnold’s situation, and that portion of the CBA reads: (Author’s Note: Bolding added for emphasis of the relevant portion of the legalese)

Section 1. Accrued Seasons Calculation:
(a) For the purposes of calculating Accrued Seasons under this Agreement, a player shall receive one Accrued Season for each season during which he was on, or should have been on, full pay status for a total of six or more regular season games (which shall include any games encompassed in any injury settlement, injury grievance settlement orinjury grievance award), but which, irrespective of the player’s pay status, shall not include games for which the player was on: (i) the Exempt Commissioner Permission List, (ii) the Reserve PUP List as a result of a nonfootball injury, or (iii) a Club’s Practice Squad.

The reason Section 1(a)(i) is bolded is, obviously, because of the simple fact that Arnold is on the Exempt List, which means he is not earning credit towards an accrued season. That means that assuming he stays on the Exempt List through at least the December 15 court date, it will be impossible for him to earn an accrued season in 2026, which in turn means that upon the expiration of his contract at the end of the league year in March, he will have the exact same number of accrued seasons as he has now, which is two.

The fact that Arnold has two accrued seasons is laid out in the above screengrab from OverTheCap.com, and it’s relevant for a very important reason. That reason is that players whose contracts have expired and who have earned only two accrued seasons are exclusive rights free agents. Exclusive rights free agents, of course, have next to zero bargaining power when it comes to negotiating because their options are to play for the ERFA contract tender the team extends or to sit at home on the couch.

Thus, while the Seahawks and Arnold only agreed to a one-year contract, assuming he does not see any game action this year, the team will have the ability to bring him back again in 2027 on a league minimum contract for $1.12M.

Of course, at that point it comes down to where things stand with the legal case. If he is found guilty and given a long prison sentence, the Seahawks are out the $1.075M they paid him this season and can move on. If, however, the legal matter is resolved in his favor when the charges get dropped or he is found not guilty, then Seattle will have paid a 24-year old former first round pick $2.195M for a season of on field performance, which is a value that seems to fall right in John Schneider’s wheelhouse.

From there is where things get interesting because as noted on social media during training camp, a one-year deal for a player with two accrued seasons isn’t really a one-year deal.

Basically, assuming Arnold doesn’t play for the Seahawks in 2026 and things somehow work out in his favor during the offseason, his only option for 2027 will be to sign for whatever ERFA tender Seattle extends. Then in 2028 he’d be a restricted free agent. Restricted free agents, of course, also have limited ability to move around in free agency and very rarely sign offer sheets with other teams, making it very likely Arnold could be retained for 2028 on an original round tender for little more than $4M.

Putting all of those pieces together, it would work out to two seasons of a former first round talent for a total price tag of $6M-$7M, which could potentially prove to be a huge value.

Of course, it’s all predicated on Arnold being able to play because he’s not on the Exempt List or in prison, so it’s all speculative until a resolution is reached on the legal matter. However, for those who may have worried about the fact that it appears his contract may expire before he’s able to do anything on the field for the Seahawks, at this point the expiration of his contract in March will be almost irrelevant because with only two accrued seasons the only way he will be able to hit unrestricted free agency upon the expiration of his contract is if the Seahawks opt not to extend an ERFA tender.

Summing it all up, Arnold might not currently be under contract past 2026, but because of the CBA he’s under team control for the foreseeable future.

item.title: Legendary player, coach Mike Ditka dies at 86
item.description: Ditka was a larger-than-life figure, in Chicago and beyond.
item.content:encoded:
Hall of Famer Mike Ditka, the legendary coach of the 1985 Bears, has died. He was 86.

Via ESPN, Ditka's family announced his passing on Friday morning.

"It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka," Ditka's family said. "While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears' Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family.

"Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever."

An Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, native who played college football at Pitt, Ditka was the first tight end to be inducted into the Hall of Fame. As a rookie in 1961, he was the first tight end in NFL history to generate 1,000 receiving yards in a season.

As a player, Ditka was a member of the Bears' 1963 NFL Championship team. He also played for the 1970 Cowboys, who won Super Bowl V.

After a 12-year playing career, Ditka joined the Cowboys as an assistant coach. In 1982, he became the head coach of the Bears.

Ditka became a larger-than-life figure in Chicago, and beyond. He oozed football, and his temperament matched the intensity of the game.

The Bears fired Ditka after the 1992 season. He became head coach of the Saints in 1997. He negotiated the famous Ricky Williams trade, in which the Saints gave up all of their 1999 draft (and another first-rounder) to get the Heisman Trophy winner from Texas.

Ditka also worked for NBC and ESPN, as an analyst.

We extend our condolences to Ditka's family, friends, players, colleagues, and to the Bears and their fans.

item.title: How many Super Bowl rings does Mike Ditka have? Coaching record, playoff wins and more
item.description: Mike Ditka is one of the most iconic figures in football. Here's a recap of Ditka's illustrious career.
item.content:encoded:
Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka is one of the most iconic figures in football.

His name and visage are legendary pieces of of the Chicago Bears' franchise. Every Bears fan can recognize him by his silhouette alone and with good reason.

Ditka, a first-round pick by Chicago back in the 1961 NFL draft, was an incredible tight end and important asset to the Bears in the early 1960s. He earned his five of his career Pro Bowl nods between 1961 and 1965 – all with the Bears – and won an NFL championship with the team in 1963 before he was traded to the Philadelphia Eagles in 1967.

In 1982, the star tight end made his return to Chicago – not as a player, but as a coach. What ensued was the greatest stretch of success in the franchise's history.

Here's everything to know about Ditka's historic career:

OPINION: Bears coaching job may seem attractive. History tells a different story.

Mike Ditka coaching record

Ditka took over as Bears head coach in 1982 after previous head coach Neill Armstrong (not to be confused with the astronaut, Neil Armstrong) failed to get the team more than one winning season in four years. Within two years, Ditka pulled the Bears to a .500 record. He followed that up in 1984 with the Bears' first winning season since 1979.

From 1984 to 1988, Ditka led the Bears to five straight 10-win seasons, a feat no Chicago coach before or since has been able to match.

By the time the Bears fired the iconic head coach after the 1992 season, he had compiled 106 wins – second in franchise history to only George Halas, the former player-coach/owner who moved the Bears to Chicago.

Ditka went 106-62 (.631 win percentage) as the Bears' head coach. He briefly coached the New Orleans Saints as well at the end of the '90s, going 15-33 (.313) in three years as their head coach.

In total, Ditka's career coaching record is 121-95 (.560).

BEARS COACHING RUMORS: Kliff Kingsbury, Marcus Freeman on list of potential Chicago hires

Mike Ditka playoff wins

Ditka first led the Bears to the playoffs in 1984. He brought Chicago back to the postseason six more times over the next eight years.

In total, he won six playoff games in his coaching career. The most iconic of those wins was the 1985 Super Bowl, which remains the Bears' only Super Bowl win in franchise history. Ditka's 1985 Bears team is synonymous with defense.

Ditka's other Bears teams were not as successful in the postseason, and he finished his coaching career with a 6-6 playoff record.

How many Super Bowl rings does Mike Ditka have?

Ditka has a total of three Super Bowl rings.

He won one as a player in Super Bowl VI with the 1971 Dallas Cowboys. He won another – Super Bowl XII – as an assistant coach with the 1977 Cowboys.

Ditka's third ring is the one he's most known for: His Super Bowl XX win as the head coach of the Bears.

He is one of only two people to win a Super Bowl as a player, assistant coach and head coach. (Raiders legend Tom Flores is the other.)

NFL PLAYOFF PREDICTIONS: Who will win AFC championship, NFC championship, Super Bowl 59?

Mike Ditka Hall of Fame induction year

Ditka was inducted to the Pro Football Hall of Fame as a player in 1988, which was 16 years after his playing career ended and during his stint as Bears head coach.

Ditka is also a member of the College Football Hall of Fame as part of its Class of 1986.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Key matchups to exploit in Week 5
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Ray Garvin highlights some key matchups to exploit in Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
I’m betting on Detroit’s passing game this week, and I want a piece of Arizona’s response, too. We’ve also got a receiving back who doesn’t need carries to help us and a couple of pass catchers whose roles fit what the defense gives up.

Let’s get into it.

Jared Goff, QB, Detroit Lions at Arizona Cardinals

Say what you want about Detroit’s defense. We’ll get to that when we talk about Michael Wilson. But this Lions offense gets an Arizona defense that has been terrible against the pass, and I like this spot a lot.

Goff enters this game with 1,214 passing yards, nine touchdowns and no interceptions. Arizona has already allowed 11 passing touchdowns and a 114.9 opponent passer rating through four games. There is opportunity here for this entire passing attack.

The Cardinals’ 66.4% two-high rate gives Detroit a reason to work underneath, but that doesn’t mean Goff won’t have his shots. Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta can keep the chains moving. Jameson Williams gives them the chance to turn one completion into a big play. This could be a good spot for him to get going, too.

And Jahmyr Gibbs is going to be involved on the ground and through the air. His presence doesn’t take me off Goff. It gives this offense another way to keep Arizona stressed.

I don’t need another 50-attempt game. Goff can be efficient, create explosive plays and still have a monster fantasy day without throwing on every possession.

I have him at QB2 this week, with more than 300 projected passing yards and two passing touchdowns. That tells you where I stand. I’m not treating Goff as a streaming option here. I’m starting him with confidence.

RJ Harvey, RB, Denver Broncos at Los Angeles Chargers

We know Harvey isn’t going to carry the ball a ton. He has run it 12 times this season. If you’re waiting for him to suddenly become a 20-carry back, you’re looking for the wrong thing.

His involvement in the receiving game is why I want to talk about him.

Harvey has caught 20 passes for 132 yards across three appearances, including 10 catches last week. Denver is finding ways to get him the football, and those receptions count just the same whether they come on a designed screen or a quick outlet from Bo Nix.

The Chargers have allowed running backs to account for 21.6% of the targets against them, the eighth-highest share through four weeks. That fits what Harvey is already doing. Swings, quick outs and screens have been part of his receiving work, giving Nix options without needing to push the ball downfield.

Now, the 10-catch game isn’t the baseline. Harvey’s route participation is only 33.8%, and J.K. Dobbins still has a role near the goal line. We can like the receiving involvement without pretending Harvey has taken over this backfield.

But if I’m choosing between Harvey and a back who needs a touchdown to save his afternoon, I’m interested in the guy catching passes.

He’s a stronger play in full PPR, but I’m considering him at flex in half-PPR, too. The carries aren’t the selling point — the receiving work is.

Luther Burden III, WR, Chicago Bears at Green Bay Packers

Chicago is a bit of a rolling crapshoot right now.

What are we getting from Tyson Bagent? How productive will the rushing attack be? Which pass catcher gets the opportunities? I’m not going to act like we have clean answers to all of that.

What I do like is what Burden has earned.

Through four weeks, he has a 22% target share and a 28.2% first-read share. This hasn’t been the massive, explosive breakout people were waiting for, but Chicago is making him a meaningful part of the offense. That matters more to me than whether he has delivered the highlight-reel performance yet.

More than half of his alignment has come from the slot, and Green Bay has played zone at a 73.6% rate. Burden’s work on digs, quick outs and shallow crosses gives Ben Johnson ways to get him involved without asking Bagent to repeatedly make difficult throws downfield.

Wide receivers have also accounted for two-thirds of the targets against the Packers. There should be opportunities for Chicago’s receivers, even if we can’t guarantee how they get distributed.

Could this turn into a Kalif Raymond game? Sure. That’s part of the frustration with trying to pin down this offense.

Still, Burden’s target involvement gives me something tangible to trust. I like him as a flex against Green Bay, especially over a receiver whose entire case depends on connecting on one deep ball.

Michael Wilson, WR, Arizona Cardinals vs. Detroit Lions

Michael Wilson is the real deal. This Lions pass defense has not been.

That’s where I’m starting.

You don’t earn 17 targets by accident. And Wilson’s broader usage tells us this isn’t just about chasing one busy afternoon. He has a 94.4% route participation rate, a 28.9% target share and a 36.8% first-read share through four weeks.

Arizona is putting him on the field and looking for him. He has become a difference-maker for this offense, and I don’t expect the Cardinals to move away from that against Detroit.

The Lions have allowed 11 passing touchdowns and a 110.4 opponent passer rating. If Goff and the Detroit offense have the day I’m projecting, Arizona will need answers. I expect Wilson and Trey McBride to be central to that response.

McBride’s matchup is excellent, too. Tight ends have accounted for 32.3% of the targets against Detroit. But there is room for both players to produce. We don’t have to manufacture a Marvin Harrison Jr. breakout to find someone who can take advantage of this defense.

Losing Paris Johnson Jr. on the offensive line is a concern. I’m not dismissing what that means for protection. But Wilson can work at different depths, and his hitches, curls and intermediate routes give Arizona ways to involve him without waiting on a deep shot.

I’m playing Wilson with full confidence. The matchup helps, but the role is what makes this a strong recommendation.

T.J. Hockenson, TE, Minnesota Vikings at New Orleans Saints

Hockenson has felt off the fantasy radar for a while. Then you watch Minnesota make him a priority, and suddenly, you remember how useful this guy can be.

The connection with Kyler Murray last week caught my attention. Even if Justin Jefferson returns, I don’t think that means Hockenson’s involvement just disappears.

There will be more target competition, that’s fair. But Hockenson has a 23.6% target share and a 28.1% first-read share through four weeks. Minnesota has been looking for him, and this opponent gives the Vikings reasons to keep doing it.

Tight ends have received 32.2% of the targets against New Orleans, the third-highest share in the league. The Saints have also used Cover 3 on 43.6% of their charted passing plays. Hockenson’s short and intermediate work gives him opportunities to find space underneath that coverage.

I expect Brian Flores’ defense to make life difficult for New Orleans. But that doesn’t mean we need Minnesota to throw all afternoon for Hockenson to contribute. A handful of catches can matter at a position where we’re often hoping our starter gets involved at all.

I like Hockenson as a starting option here. Check the injury news, but don’t assume Jefferson returning erases the connection we just saw.

item.title: Mike Ditka's defining coaching moments: Remembering the Bears legend
item.description: Mike Ditka's football legacy includes an 11-year run as the Chicago Bears coach that was highlighted by winning the 1985 Super Bowl.
item.content:encoded:
Mike Ditka once said he was going to live to be 150 years old. The legendary former Chicago Bears coach and Hall of Fame tight end had a very specific (and very Ditka appropriate) reason whenever asked why he wanted that to be the case.

"There’s a lot of people I haven’t (ticked) off yet," Ditka declared in an interview published by the Los Angeles Times in 1996, "so I want to get them all."

Ditka died on Friday, Oct. 9, his family announced. He was 86 years old.

"It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka," his family said in a statement. "While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears' Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever."

Ditka's legacy in football, and especially the role he played as a player and coach with the Bears, will endure long after his life. He will be remembered as one of the seminal figures in league history, both due to his exploits as a revolutionary pass-catching tight end for the Bears in the 1960s and his 11-year run as coach with the franchise.

Here is a look back at some of the defining coaching moments from Ditka's remarkable career:

Mike Ditka's best coaching moments

Mike Ditka’s coaching roots: Tom Landry and the Dallas Cowboys

Mike Ditka got his coaching start in 1972 working as a special teams and tight ends coach for the Dallas Cowboys under legendary coach Tom Landry, who had helped rejuvenate the end of Ditka’s playing career. Ditka, who won the Super Bowl as a player with the Cowboys in the 1971-1972 season, eventually won a Super Bowl with the Cowboys as an assistant coach in 1977. 

Chicago Bears hire Mike Ditka

During the 1981 season, Ditka famously wrote a letter to his former coach and Bears owner George Halas expressing a desire to one day be considered for the team's head coaching position despite Ditka's acrimonious exit from Chicago as a player. Halas then hired Ditka ahead of the 1982 season to replace former coach Neill Armstrong after back-to-back losing seasons.

FROM THE ARCHIVES: Mike Ditka looks back on greatness of Bears' 1985 Super Bowl team

Mike Ditka leads Chicago Bears back to NFL playoffs

Ditka went 3-6 during the 1982 season that was shortened by a players’ strike and improved to 8-8 in his first full season as Bears’ coach in 1983. But Ditka’s breakthrough arrived in 1984, when he led the Bears to their first postseason win in more than 20 years. Chicago lost in the NFC championship game to the San Francisco 49ers, the eventual Super Bowl champions.

Mike Ditka wins Super Bowl with 1985 Bears

The 1985 NFL season is the seminal moment of Mike Ditka’s coaching career, as he led the Bears to a 15-1 regular season and then a win over the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX. Ditka became the first person in NFL history to win a Super Bowl as a player, assistant coach and head coach, and also the first head coach to win a Super Bowl for a team in which he played for. He is the only person to take part in the Bears' last two titles – the 1963 NFL championship as a player and 1986 as coach. 

Helped by future Pro Football Hall of Famers such as running back Walter Payton, linebacker Mike Singletary and the famed ‘46’ defense created by coordinator and antagonist Buddy Ryan, Ditka’s quotable personality and trademark intensity, combined with his success with the Bears, turned "Da Coach" into one of the NFL’s most unforgettable characters. The 1985 Bears are widely considered one of the greatest teams in league history. 

Mike Ditka’s last playoff run

The same year Mike Ditka was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame for what he did as a player also coincided with him winning NFL coach of the year for the second time in 1988. Ditka, despite suffering a heart attack during the season, took the Bears to the NFC championship game for the third time in five seasons. The playoff run included a win over Ryan, who was coaching the Philadelphia Eagles and had a rivalry with Ditka dating back to their time working together in Chicago.

Mike Ditka coaching record

  • 121-95 overall record in 14 seasons (11 in Chicago, 3 in New Orleans)
  • Second-most wins in Bears history (106) behind only George Halas
  • 1 Super Bowl win
  • 3 NFC championship game appearances
  • 7 NFL playoff appearances
  • 6 NFC Central division titles

item.title: The 49ers are running into the stingiest defense in the NFL
item.description: Three numbers to watch heading into Week 5 between the 49ers and Seahawks
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are looking for a perfect first leg against the NFC West with a win on Sunday in the Pacific Northwest against the Seattle Seahawks.

After defeating the Rams and Arizona, the 49ers sit atop the NFC West, but the 3-1 Seahawks are within shouting distance, and an early division lead is on the line. A win would give San Francisco the tiebreaker over all three NFC West foes in the early goings and a two-game lead in the win column. 

But Seattle was a tricky game (twice) in the ladder half of 2025 for the 49ers, and Sunday could be the same with Seattle getting Sam Darnold back a couple of weeks ago. And while Darnold will lead the Seattle offense, the main attraction of the Seahawks is that defense.

Let’s take a closer look at the Seattle defense with this week’s numbers to know:

246.8

Yards per game. The Seahawks defense allows 246.8 yards per game, the best in the league.

The Denver Broncos defense was just a Week 4 appetizer for the Week 5 main course: Mike Macdonald’s elite Seattle defense. 

Entering Week 5, only two defenses have allowed fewer than 1,000 yards. After Sunday, the 49ers will have played both of those teams. The 49ers offense put up 379 yards in Week 1 against the Los Angeles Rams, the current season-high against Los Angeles, but since then, the Rams have allowed 611 in three games, bringing their season total to 990 yards allowed. Only one team has allowed fewer yards: the Seahawks.

While the 49ers offense has gained more than 300 yards in all four games this season, Seattle has allowed more than 300 yards once, last week when the Los Angeles Chargers gained 301. And just as the 49ers’ ability to gain yards has led to the second-highest point output through four weeks (122), Seattle’s ability to hold offenses has kept teams to the fifth-fewest points (73).

In simpler terms, Sunday will be an immovable object versus an unstoppable force.

Now, where will the 49ers find the firepower against Seattle’s defense? Mike Evans is banged up, and unlike Week 1, the 49ers will be without Demarcus Robinson and De’Zhaun Stribling. The receiver injuries will be familiar, though, as the position group was hurt last season when Seattle dominated the 49ers offense in Week 17 and the playoffs. 

1

Touchdowns. The Seattle defense has allowed one rushing touchdown this season, the second-fewest allowed in the league.

While the passing game has been responsible for 11 of the 49ers’ 16 touchdowns this season, Christian McCaffrey on the ground remains the biggest scoring threat on the 49ers’ offense, especially inside the red zone.

Seattle’s defense has been susceptible to the run this season, allowing 100+ rushing yards in two of its four games. But because Seattle is so good everywhere else on defense, that slight issue against the run hasn’t hurt much. 

But this game might be decided by how often the 49ers offense can get into the red zone. Seattle has allowed the second-fewest red zone entries with nine through four games. Despite the few entries, Seattle has allowed five touchdowns, a 66.7 touchdown rate tied for the tenth-highest.

Only one of those red zone touchdowns has come on the ground. And that’s where McCaffrey comes into play. All 27 of his rushing touchdowns have come inside the red zone, and all four of his rushing touchdowns in 2026 were one-yard scores. It’s safe to say that Seattle’s defense won’t face a red zone weapon like McCaffrey outside the two games against the 49ers.

It’s tough to move the ball against Seattle’s defense, and it’s especially hard to score on the ground. McCaffrey could be the answer to that threat. 

7-3

Record. The 49ers are 7-3 (including playoffs) against the Seahawks under Brock Purdy.

If Purdy can continue his current form against this Seattle defense, it would be a statement game we look back on to solidify an MVP case at the end of the season.

Purdy did have his struggles against the Seahawks in 2025, averaging 181.3 passing yards in three games against Seattle, in a season where he averaged 240 yards per game. Even after success in his first try against Macdonald’s version of the Seahawks when Purdy threw for three touchdowns leading a 49ers win, all three of Purdy’s losses to the Seahawks have come under Macdonald’s tenure.

But that doesn’t mean Purdy hasn’t had success against Macdonald. Purdy has led the 49ers to two wins against Seattle and has looked good in both. The first being the aforementioned three-touchdown game from Purdy, picking up a win in Week 6 of the 2024 season, but he also led the game-winning drive in Week 1 last season, capping off a two-touchdown day.

Purdy’s dominance of the Seahawks was more of a Pete Carroll thing than it was a Macdonald. And while the Seahawks’ head coach has had Purdy’s number dating back to Christmas Day 2023, Purdy has had his fair share of success as well. 

Sunday, however, Macdonald and the Seahawks defense will have to face Purdy in the middle of one of the best stretches of his career.

item.title: Former Saints, Bears Coach and NFL Legend Mike Ditka Dies at 86
item.description: The Hall of Famer leaves behind a lasting legacy as one of the NFL’s most recognizable players and coaches.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL has lost another legend. Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka has died at the age of 86.

One of the most recognizable figures in professional football, Ditka built a remarkable career spanning decades as both a player and head coach. Known for his fiery personality, toughness and passion for the game, Ditka became synonymous with the Chicago Bears before later taking over as head coach of the New Orleans Saints.

Ditka’s greatest coaching achievement came during the 1985 season, when he led the Bears to a dominant 15-1 regular-season record and a victory over the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX. Chicago’s legendary defense and Ditka’s larger-than-life personality helped make that team one of the most memorable in NFL history.

Before his coaching career, Ditka established himself as one of the league’s premier tight ends. Selected in the first round (fifth overall) by the Bears in the 1961 NFL Draft, he played 12 seasons with Chicago, the Philadelphia Eagles and the Dallas Cowboys.

Ditka served as head coach of the Bears for 11 seasons (1982-92) before returning to the sidelines in 1997 when the Saints hired him to lead the franchise. His arrival in New Orleans generated excitement among fans hoping the Hall of Famer could bring the same championship success he had achieved in Chicago.

However, Ditka’s three seasons with the Saints were far less successful. New Orleans finished 6-10 in both 1997 and 1998 before falling to 3-13 in 1999. He compiled a 15-33 record and failed to lead the franchise to a playoff appearance. Following the disappointing 1999 season, Ditka and the Saints parted ways, ending his NFL coaching career.

Despite his struggles in New Orleans, Ditka’s overall accomplishments remained significant. He finished his 14-year head coaching career with a 121-95 regular-season record, including 106 victories with Chicago.

Ditka was one of the few figures in NFL history to win championships as a player, assistant coach and head coach. In 1986, Ditka was enshrined into the College Football Hall of Fame and in 1988, he made history as the first tight end inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Affectionately known as “Iron Mike,” Ditka was a legendary figure both on the field and on the sidelines, leaving behind a lasting legacy in NFL history.

item.title: Mike Ditka coaching tree includes Jim Harbaugh and Sean Payton
item.description: The Hall of Fame players spent more than a decade on NFL sidelines as a head coach. Here are some the biggest names in his coaching tree.
item.content:encoded:
Mike Ditka, who died Friday, Oct. 9, at the age of 86, spent decades as a fixture in the game of football. The Hall of Fame tight end was a pioneer as a player after going fifth overall in the 1961 NFL Draft to the Chicago Bears. As a rookie, he became the first tight end in NFL history to surpass 1,000 yards receiving. He'd never repeat that feat but made five Pro Bowls over a 12-year career with the Bears, Philadelphia Eagles, and Dallas Cowboys.

After retiring following the 1972 NFL season, Ditka immediately began his coaching career with the Cowboys under Hall of Famer Tom Landry. That started a 23-year coaching career, highlighted by his time as head coach of the Bears from 1982 to 1992. Ditka returned to the sidelines from 1997 through 1999 as coach of the New Orleans Saints.

Ditka didn't create an expansive coaching tree of the likes of Landry, Bill Walsh or Bill Parcells, but he did oversee multiple future NFL coaches. Here's what his coaching tree looked like:

Mike Ditka coaching tree

Buddy Ryan

Ryan pioneered the 46 defense in Chicago as the defensive coordinator under Ditka from 1982 to 1985. Ryan himself has an expansive coaching tree that he developed, including his twin sons Rob and Rex, Jeff Fisher, Mike Singletary, Leslie Frazier, Ron Rivera, Jim Schwartz and Wade Phillips.

Vince Tobin

Tobin, the uncle of Cincinnati Bengals de facto general manager Duke Tobin, succeeded Ryan as the Bears' defensive coordinator in 1986. He'd serve in that role through 1992 and later became the Arizona Cardinals' head coach in 1996. From 1996 through Week 8 of the 2000 NFL season, Tobin coached 71 games with the Cardinals and went 28-43.

Dave McGinnis

McGinnis had a 43-year coaching career but got his first break in the NFL as a linebackers coach under Ditka from 1986 through 1992. He remained in that position with the Bears through 1995 before becoming the Cardinals' defensive coordinator in 1996 under Tobin. McGinnis later took over for Tobin in 2000 after his firing and remained the team's head coach through the end of the 2003 season. McGinnis went 17-40 in his time as the Cardinals' head coach.

Jack Del Rio

Del Rio had an 11-year NFL career with the Saints, Kansas City Chiefs, Cowboys and Minnesota Vikings. He retired after the 1996 NFL season and got his first coaching job as the assistant strength coach with the Saints under Ditka in 1997. In 1998, he was the team's linebackers coach.

After stops in Baltimore and Carolina, Del Rio became the head coach of the Jacksonville Jaguars from 2003 to 2011 and he went 68-71 in the regular season and 1-2 in the playoffs. Four years later, he was named the head coach of the Las Vegas (then-Oakland) Raiders. In three seasons leading the Raiders, Del Rio went 25-23 in the regular season and 0-1 in the playoffs.

NFL coaches who played for Mike Ditka

Jeff Fisher

Fisher played under Ditka as a defensive back in 1982 and 1984, appearing in 25 total games. He never coached under Ditka, instead getting his start under Ryan. Fisher spent 22 years as an NFL head coach with the Houston/Tennessee Oilers/Titans as well as the St. Louis/Los Angeles Rams. He's tied with Bill Belichick and Dan Reeves for the most regular season losses in NFL history with 165.

Mike Singletary

Singletary played nearly his entire NFL career with Ditka as his head coach. The Bears' second round pick in the 1981 NFL Draft made 10 Pro Bowls and seven All-Pro teams from 1981 through 1992. He was the San Francisco 49ers' head coach from Week 8 of the 2008 season through Week 16 of the 2010 season. In that 40-game span, he went 18-22 as a coach.

Ron Rivera

Rivera spent his entire playing career under Ditka as a Bears linebacker from 1984 to 1992. He spent 13 years as a head coach in the NFL with the Carolina Panthers and Washington Commanders. He went 102-103-2 in the regular season and 3-5 in the playoffs as a coach, highlighted by an NFC conference championship in 2015.

Jim Harbaugh

Harbaugh was the Bears' first-round pick in the 1987 NFL Draft and spent six seasons under Ditka in Chicago before stints with the Indianapolis Colts, Baltimore Ravens, and Los Angeles (then-San Diego) Chargers. Harbaugh began coaching in the NFL in 2011 with the 49ers. He spent four seasons there and went 44-19-1 and 5-3 in the playoffs, including an NFC title in 2012. He returned to the NFL in 2024 as the Chargers' coach.

Leslie Frazier

Frazier had a five-year playing career as a Bears cornerback from 1981 to 1985 which included four seasons under Ditka. He got his first NFL coaching job with the Philadelphia Eagles in 1999 and eventually became head coach of the Minnesota Vikings in Week 12 of the 2010 NFL season. Over the next four seasons, Frazier went 21-32-1 as head coach and 0-1 in the playoffs.

Sean Payton

Payton played for Ditka for three games during the NFL Players Association strike in 1987, his lone NFL experience.

“It was just a month but Ditka left a big impression,” Payton told Sports Illustrated in 2015. "I was a Chicago kid; I knew him as a fan before I found myself in pads being yelled at by him. He’s a big guy. And you knew what kind of player he was—ferocious. And he had that mustache that’d freeze, and was it water? Or was it spit? I was scared to death. But what stayed with me was his intensity."

Payton is more considered part of Parcells' coaching tree due to his time as the Cowboys' assistant head coach and quarterbacks coach from 2003 to 2005. Starting in 2006, Payton spent 15 years as the Saints' head coach and went 152-89 in the regular and 9-8 in the playoffs, highlighted by a Super Bowl win in 2009. After a year off, Payton returned to the coaching ranks with the Denver Broncos.

item.title: What teams did Mike Ditka play for? Hall of Fame tight end's college, NFL stats
item.description: Mike Ditka was the first tight end elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Here's every team he played for, and his stats.
item.content:encoded:
Pro Football Hall of FamerMike Ditka was the first tight end elected to Canton in 1988 following a legendary NFL career that spanned 12 seasons and three teams, most notably with the Chicago Bears.

Ditka helped evolve the tight end position into a high-volume offensive weapon. According to the Pro Football Hall of Fame, Ditka "introduced a new dimension to the tight end position that once was viewed primarily as an assignment for a tough, talented blocker. Ditka proved to be a superior blocker, but he also became one of the first tight ends to catch a large number of passes."

Here's every team that Mike Ditka played for, from his collegiate days in Pittsburgh to the NFL:

Where did Mike Ditka go to college?

Ditka, a Pennsylvania native, stayed close to home and played collegiate football at the University of Pittsburgh, less than 30 miles away from his hometown. Ditka played three seasons at Pittsburgh (1958-1960), all under coach John Michelosen. Ditka led the team in receiving three consecutive years as a tight end. He also played defensive line.

During his senior season, Ditka was unanimously named to the College Football All-America team after recording 11 receptions for 229 yards and two touchdowns (10 starts) and he finished sixth in Heisman Trophy voting. In 30 career games for Pittsburgh, Ditka caught 45 passes for 730 yards and seven touchdowns.

Ditka was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1986. His No. 89 jersey was retired by the Panthers in 1997 and he was inducted into the University of Pittsburgh Athletics Hall of Fame in its inaugural class in 2018.

Mike Ditka playing for Pitt circa 1960 pic.twitter.com/Mz3zXpQMzh

— Pittsburgh Sports Memories (@PittsburghSpo18) July 21, 2024

Which teams did Mike Ditka play for in the NFL?

Ditka was drafted by the Chicago Bears with the fifth overall pick in the 1961 NFL draft. He was also drafted by the Houston Oilers with the eighth overall pick of the 1961 AFL draft, but he signed with the Bears.

Chicago Bears (1961-66)

Ditka played for the Bears for six seasons and made 84 consecutive starts from 1961 to 1966. In his first season with the Bears, Ditka recorded 58 receptions for 1,076 yards and 12 touchdowns, tied for the most receiving touchdowns by a Bears rookie (Harlon Hill, 1954). Ditka was named the NFL AP Rookie of the Year in 1961 and earned Pro Bowl honors.

Ditka earned All-Pro honors five straight seasons (1962-66, including first-team honors in 1963 and 1964) and Pro Bowl nods five consecutive years with the Bears (1961–65). He helped the team win the 1963 NFL championship. In 84 career games (all starts) for the Bears across six seasons, Ditka recorded 316 receptions for 4,503 yards and 34 touchdowns.

Philadelphia Eagles (1967-68)

Ditka couldn't reach a contract extension with Bears owner and head coach George Halas and was subsequently traded to the Philadelphia Eagles in April 1967. Ditka's production dipped in his first season with the Eagles due to injury, only appearing in nine games (six starts). He had 26 receptions for 274 yards and two touchdowns. In 20 games with the Eagles across two seasons, Ditka appeared in 20 games (12 starts) and recorded 39 receptions for 385 yards and four touchdowns.

Dallas Cowboys (1969-72)

Ditka was traded to the Dallas Cowboys in January 1969. In his first season with the Cowboys, Ditka appeared in 12 games (four starts) and had 17 receptions for 268 yards and three touchdowns, despite being behind fellow tight end Pettis Norman on the depth chart. He remained behind Norman in 1970 and posted a career-low eight receptions for 98 yards and no touchdowns in 14 games (no starts).

Ditka remained a backup in 1971 — this time to tight end Billy Truax — but he had 30 receptions for 360 yards and one touchdown in 14 appearances (four starts). The Cowboys advanced to the Super Bowl for the second straight season and defeated the Miami Dolphins 24-3 at Tulane Stadium in New Orleans. Ditka had two receptions for 28 yards and one touchdown, in addition to a 17-yard run, in the Super Bowl VI win.

Ditka started all 14 games for his fourth and final season with the Cowboys and recorded 17 receptions for 198 yards and one touchdown.

When did Mike Ditka retire?

Ditka announced his retirement after the 1972 season on March 1, 1973, following 12 seasons in the NFL. He retired with 427 receptions — a league record for a tight end at the time — 5,812 yards and 43 touchdowns. Ditka was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988 and became the first tight end to make it to Canton.

"In life, many men have talent, but talent in itself is no accomplishment," Ditka said during his enshrinement speech. "Excellence in football and excellence in life is bred when men recognize their opportunities and then pursue them with a passion, and I think that sums up what the players of the National Football League and NFL Hall of Fame stand for. They recognize an opportunity and they went after it."

Ditka immediately went into coaching after his retirement and was hired as an assistant by his former Cowboys coach, Tom Landry. He went on to become the head coach of the Chicago Bears (1982-92) and New Orleans Saints (1997-99).
