item.title: Giants-Commanders matchup: When the Giants have the football
item.description: What the Giants’ offense must do to earn a divisional road victory.
item.content:encoded:
The 3-1 Giants travel to Washington to play the 1-3 Commanders, who will receive starting quarterback Jayden Daniels back. The 2024 Rookie of the Year is returning from a dislocated left elbow. Washington is favored by three-and-a-half points, and the Over/Under is set at 43.5 points.

The Commanders are returning from London, where the Indianapolis Colts defeated them 30-13; Washington had to play rookie third-stringer Athan Kaliakmanis at quarterback after Marcus Mariota suffered a knee injury in the first half. Washington has won the last four matchups against the Giants. New York leads the series 108-75-5.

Team statistics

(And a persepctive on the Giants’ pass rush)

The Commanders surrender the third-most points (122) and the 15th-most yards allowed (1,344). They allow the eighth-most passing yards (970) and are tied for the most passing touchdowns surrendered, with 11. Dan Quinn’s unit, coached by first-year defensive coordinator Daronte Jones, has the sixth-best run defense in the league per yard allowed; they allowed 374 yards through four games, for 4 yards per carry.

Quinn’s team has the fewest penalties accepted this year — they have only 19 penalties against them. They are third in blitz rate, with a 36.8% blitz rate and sixth in pressure percentage. The Giants have been a topic of discussion in pressure and sacks this season, since they rank last in both through four games. Here are some thoughts on that:

Defensive personnel

As for the Commanders, they’ve been pressuring opposing quarterbacks. Odafe Oweh and Darone Payne both had four pressures against Daniel Jones and the Colts. Oweh and Payne lead the team with 12 pressures, and K’Lavon Chaisson has 11. Javon Kinlaw, Charles Omenihu, and Dorance Armstrong each have six pressures, while star rookie linebacker Sonny Styles has five with a sack.

Washington has a solid front that lacks star-power names other than Daron Payne. Kinlaw and Omenihu play alongside Payne, with Tim Settle and Shy Tuttle as rotational defensive linemen.

Oweh and Chaisson are the primary edge rushers, with long-time Quinn favorite Dorance Armstrong as the third rusher. Rookie Joshua Josephs has also played 53 snaps over four games. Linebacker Frankie Luvu has four pressures on the year, but he missed Weeks 2 and 3. Luvu plays a hybrid linebacker/edge role; he returned in Week 4 against the Colts. Second-year sixth-round pick Kain Medrano, out of UCLA, has played in Luvu’s absence, and he recorded an important interception in Washington’s impressive Week 3 win over Seattle.

Sonny Styles is the fulcrum of the defense and is playing quality football.

Arvell Reese’s former teammate is a good football player that the Giants’ offense must account for on Sunday. Off-season signing Leo Chenal suffered a neck fracture in Week 3 and is out.

Washington likes to use three-safety sets. A three-safety defense against the heavier Giants’ offense could struggle against the run. Safety Percy Butler played 19 of his 32 snaps on Sunday. While Quan Martin and Jeremy Reaves played 59 and 53, respectively. Safety Nick Cross was out the last two weeks; early optimism suggests he may play on Sunday.

The cornerback position is manned by Rasul Douglas and Amik Robertson. Mike Sainristil struggled early in the season and was benched. The former second-round pick played just five snaps against the Colts. 2025 second-round pick Tre Amos is on the I.R. with a fractured fibula. Fabian Moreau played 26 snaps against the Colts. Washington’s corner room is being held down by journeymen.

The matchup

With Jameis Winston as the listed starter, the Giants are using a heavier personnel package (more than 11) at a 62% rate, with 27% of that being 22 personnel, meaning two tight ends, a running back, and Patrick Ricard at full-back. Of the 62%, only 12% is 12 personnel. The Giants are a beefy team that wants to establish the run. This will lead to more base looks from Washington, which removes a nickel and puts Tim Settle on the line of scrimmage between Daron Payne and an edge defender.

The Colts ran 11% at a high 47% rate and 12 personnel at a rate of 42%. The Giants will be a different challenge for the Commanders, but can New York effectively establish the run against Washington? The Colts ran well against Washington’s nickel looks; Jonathan Taylor averaged 4.8 yards per carry, and Seth McGowan averaged 5.2 yards per carry.

The Giants, though, have struggled to run the football. They averaged 3.1 yards per carry against the Cardinals, and the running backs averaged 3.9 yards per carry against the Titans — both wins. New York should look to keep the run defense honest with misdirections, counters, or jet sweeps, as they did in Week 3 with Darnell Mooney, which resulted in a nine-yard gain. Getting to that early, against an aggressive defense like Washington, could work for a chunk gain; or perhaps a few drives in after showing jet-motion from 12 personnel.

New York used EMPTY 13 personnel to spread the defense out and create mismatches for the No. 3 (innermost) receiver against zone coverage. New York scored two touchdowns in the red zone this way on Sunday, and it was refreshing to see the success of the strategy for the run-heavy team with a second-string quarterback who has struggled in the red zone.

The Commanders have more athletic ability at their second level than the Cardinals, though. The Giants will likely go to these looks, but it may not be as successful as it was in Week 4. Malik Nabers should remain the focal point of the passing attack, and his usage should expand across the formation.

Malachi Fields is an asset on the outside in a winnable matchup when up against Robertson, who is 5’8. Robertson starts on the right side and has been Quinn’s best cornerback, but the size difference is noteworthy. Robertson is aggressive by the line of scrimmage; New York could look for a double-move or fake screen to bait a mistake and create explosive plays off the top.

New York can look to their matchups when facing man coverage, specifically Fields, Isaiah Likely, and Malik Nabers. Far-hash throws are another thing the Giants could use to attack Quinn if the veteran coach opts for Cover-6 looks that leave the deep curl/flat vacated to the field. I would love it if the Giants leaned on Cam Skattebo a bit more in this game. Najee Harris and Skattebo essentially split time and touches until the former fumbled.

Then there’s Tyrone Tracy Jr. The Giants should keep using him in the package between the 10-25 yard line on the opponent’s side of the field. New York tried to run RB-Corner routes out of shotgun against Cover 3; it’s a look they used in the preseason with Tracy too.

Isaiah Likely’s usage should remain — keep using him in the short/intermediate parts of the field as an easy target with high-YAC upside.

Final thoughts

The Commanders are a respectable team who, much like the Giants, are bitten by the injury bug. A divisional road win is incredibly valuable. The Giants’ offense must play mistake-free football. Winston must operate with better discernment and play poised in the pocket, while the backs need to hold onto the football. It won’t be easy, but I have the Giants winning, 20-16.

item.title: Mike Ditka, Chicago Bears Hall of Fame legend, dies at 86
item.description: Ditka was best known for leading the 1985 Chicago Bears to the only Super Bowl title in franchise history.
item.content:encoded:
Of all the quotes attributed to Mike Ditka over the years, there's one in particular that stands out when it comes to the way he lived his life in football.

"Living in the past is for cowards," the football legend once said. "If you live in the past, you die in the past."

Like many other things Ditka said, it was brash and impulsive. It made no pretensions about being delicate or polite.

It was, however, an accurate depiction of the way Ditka kept progressing and evolving in over 60 years of being involved with the sport. He succeeded more than he failed, but he claimed that didn't matter much.

“Success isn't permanent and failure isn't fatal," went one of Ditka's other famous quotes.

Ditka died on Friday, his family announced. He was 86.

Jarrett Payton, Walter Payton's son, announced the news on Chicago's 104.3 The Score. Payton shared a statement from the Ditka family on X:

It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka. While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears' Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever. With love and gratitude, The Ditka Family

Legendary Bears coach Mike Ditka has passed away, @paytonsun just learned. pic.twitter.com/2N821GERZS

— 104.3 The Score (@thescorechicago) October 9, 2026

In a football career that spanned nearly five decades, Ditka earned induction into both the College Football and Pro Football Hall of Fames, won NFL championships as a player, an assistant and a head coach, the latter coming in the 1985 season, when he led the Chicago Bears to its first and still only Super Bowl title.

The 1985 championship launched Ditka into a new level of fame. He cashed checks for pitching a wide variety of products, was lovingly lampooned on a classic "Saturday Night Live" sketch and became the closest thing the Chicago sporting scene has ever had to a patron saint.

But while Chicago's triumph over New England in January 1986 remained the high point in Ditka's career, it was far from the only highlight. 

Indeed, few men have experienced Ditka's level or breadth of success in the game. His coaching days were preceded by a Hall of Fame playing career with the Bears and Cowboys, then followed with successful ventures in both broadcasting and business. In his later years, Ditka started the "Gridiron Greats Assistance Fund," an organization designed to help struggling ex-players who hadn't been rewarded as handsomely by the game as he was.  

From Pennsylvania to Chicago  

Though he looked as if he was from one of Chicago's many Polish neighborhoods, Ditka was born "Michael Dyczko" on Oct. 18, 1939 in Carnegie, Pennsylvania. The son of a welder, he played high school football in Aliquippa and his stardom in steel country gave him the "Iron Mike" nickname that would stick for decades after he left the state.

After a successful collegiate career at Pitt, Ditka was drafted by the Bears with the fifth overall pick in the 1961 NFL Draft. He won that season's Rookie of the Year award and was a key part of Chicago's 1963 NFL championship team under George Halas, the last Bears team to win a title until Halas hired Ditka to return the team to glory in the '80s. 

Ditka was traded to the Eagles in 1967, but eventually landed in Dallas, where he won Super Bowl titles with the Cowboys both as a player (VI) and an assistant coach (XII). He and Oakland Raiders coach Tom Flores remain the only men to win Super Bowls as a player, assistant and coach. 

After nearly a decade spent as an assistant under Cowboys legend Tom Landry, Ditka sent a letter to Halas saying he was "ready" to return home and lead the Bears. Halas took him up on his offer for the 1982 season and within three seasons, Ditka took the Bears to the NFC title game. 

Ditka had a distinct coaching style

Ditka's leadership style could best be described as volatile, and his relationships with players, fellow coaches and media were far from perfect. Even though the egos belonging to Ditka and defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan could barely co-exist in the same locker room, the 1985 Bears became one of the sport's greatest teams, going 15-1 and shutting out two teams in the NFC playoffs before shellacking the Patriots 46-10 in Super Bowl XX. 

Ryan left to become the Eagles' head coach after the Super Bowl. Ditka and the drama-filled and often injured Bears never again reached the top, soon outclassed in the NFC by San Francisco, Washington and New York. In later years, members of the '85 team would come out and say Ditka should've won at least one more title with the talent he had, a charge with which the coach himself later agreed. 

Ditka was fired following the 1992 season, capping an 11-year run that saw the Bears go 106-62. He surfaced in New Orleans in 1997 for a three-year stint that would have been largely forgettable were it not for his decision to trade away all of the Saints' picks in 1999 (plus a first-rounder in 2000) for the right to move up and take Heisman Trophy winner Ricky Williams. The pair posed as a just-married couple for the cover of ESPN: The Magazine, with Williams donning a wedding dress.  

Ditka remained visible after coaching career

Following his departure from New Orleans, Ditka resumed a broadcasting career he'd started with NBC and took jobs with CBS, then ESPN. He cultivated his personality into a successful and pervasive brand, running popular restaurants in the Chicagoland area and putting his visage on everything from fine wine and bloody mary mix to salsa and giardiniera, a spicy Italian relish that is popular in the Chicagoland area. 

A staunch Republican, Ditka considered running for Illinois' open Senate seat in 2004 but ultimately decided against it. 

A Democrat named Barack Obama ended up winning the office, and Ditka, with no small amount of bitterness, would later remark that the course of American history would have been different had he decided to pursue the office.

item.title: Jets Week 5 Injury Updates: Breece Hall and Adonai Mitchell out, Mason Taylor in
item.description: Ahead of the Jets' Week 5 game against the Cleveland Browns, head coach Aaron Glenn gave some injury updates at practice on Friday, ruling out RB Breece Hall and WR Adonai Mitchell, but confirming that TE Mason Taylor is ready to play.
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of the Jets' Week 5 game against the Cleveland Browns, head coach Aaron Glenn gave some injury updates at practice on Friday...

RB Breece Hall, WR Adonai Mitchell

Hall (quad) and Mitchell (finger) have both been ruled out for Sunday's game against the Browns.

"Guys that will be out, AD Mitchell, Breece Hall, Dylan Parham, and Kiko [Mauigoa]." Glenn announced.

In Hall's absence, running back Braelon Allen got all of the touches in the backfield for the Jets against the Bears in Week 4, running for 59 yards on 14 carries.

Hall suffered the quad injury in Week 3 against the Lions, exiting in the fourth quarter.

All four players also missed last week's game.

Mitchell's finger injury, which will now sideline him for the third straight game, remains a bit of a mystery.

"Actually, he's progressing faster than we thought he would," Green explained. "We'll see how it goes moving into next week."

Green added that Mitchell did not have a procedure on the finger, and replied that he is "not a doctor" when asked if the finger was broken or fractured.

TE Mason Taylor, EDGE Kingsley Enagbare, CB Jarvis Brownlee, Jr.

"Mason [Taylor] has done a good job... Mason will be playing," Green declared when asked about the status of his second-year tight end.

Taylor (thumb) practiced on Wednesday after not playing last week.

Taylor has just two catches for -2 yards over two games, last playing in Week 2 against the Packers.

"Jarvis [Brownlee] is progressing very, very well," said Green on Friday. "He'll be a full [participant] at practice today."

The cornerback was knocked out of last week's game against the Bears with a concussion, but it appears that he'll be ready to play against the Browns on Sunday.

Meanwhile, Enagbare (knee) - who also practiced on Wednesday alongside Taylor, albeit in a limited capacity - can be considered questionable for that game.

In his first season with New York after four seasons in Green Bay, Enagbare has made nine tackles and has two sacks and a forced fumble over three games.

"I like where these guys are trending, and am looking forward to seeing them playing," the head coach said.

WR Tim Patrick

Patrick has been designated for a return to practice, as the team is opening his 21-day window to be added to the active roster from the injured reserve.

"We'll see how it goes and make a decision fairly quickly, but [Patrick] will be practicing today," Glenn shared with the media on Friday.

The veteran wideout signed with the Jets in March, but has been sidelined since the first week of practice due to a groin injury.

Last season, Patrick had 15 receptions for 187 yards and three touchdowns over 16 games (three starts) for the Jaguars.

item.title: Raiders-Patriots Week 5: 5 things to wacth
item.description: Keys to a Las Vegas upset at New England
item.content:encoded:
The 3-1 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 2-2 New England Patriots on Sunday. Kickoff is set for 10 a.m. PT. Here are five keys to victory for the Raiders:

Get turnovers:

The Raiders ran out to a 3-0 start to the season fueled by takeaways. They had a league-high nine in that stretch. They lost the turnover battle 2-0 in their loss to the Chiefs in Week 4. Thus, they need to get back on the plus side of the turnover game. This is a good matchup for them. The Patriots are tied for a league high 10 turnovers and quarterback Drake Maye has thrown seven interceptions. The Raiders have to capitalize.

Win the fourth quarter:

Fourth-quarter play was another difference in the Raiders’ Week 4 loss. In the first three games, the Raiders didn’t allow any points in the fourth quarter. They allowed 20 against the Chiefs. The Raiders must get back to finishing games.

Stop the run:

Kansas City running back Kenneth Walker had 177 yards rushing and averaged eight yards a carry last week. That has to change, but expect the Patriots to try to get Rhanondre Stevenson (has been out of practice some but has a chance to play) and TreyVeyon Henderson going early in this game.

Run the ball:

The Raiders’ running game has been lacking since Week 1. It’s an issue and they must estbalish the ground game soon.

Tight end dominance:

The Raiders’ wide-receiving group was thin to start with and now they have injuries, so the emphasis on the tight ends. Brock Bowers, Michael Mayer and Ian Thomas combined for 16 catches for 200 yards and two touchdowns last week. They will need another high-production day from the group this week.

item.title: Seahawks-49ers NFL Week 5 predictions: Jaxon Smith-Njigba will dominate again
item.description: Seattle’s star could go supernova against the 49ers. Again.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks scraped by the Los Angeles Chargers with a narrow 7-point win last week and now turn to their toughest test of the season. Their NFC West rival, the San Francisco 49ers, will come to town this week in what looks to be a narrow contest, with FanDuel Sportsbook listing the Seahawks as three-point favorites.

Let’s take a look at what it will take for the Seahawks to reassert their divisional dominance on Sunday.

1. Seattle will reestablish the JSN

I’m well aware it’s a little comical to suggest that Seahawks’ star wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba will have a “bounce back” game after he posted 76 yards on five catches last week. However, the statistical performance was below the extremely high standard he has set in 2026, and the offense felt it. That should change this week as I guarantee Sam Darnold and offensive coordinator Brian Fleury will have their minds set on getting JSN the ball more, especially considering how he dominated the 49ers last season, totaling 227 yards and a touchdown. Not to mention the 49ers are dealing with several secondary injuries, making Smith-Njigba a prime target for an impressive day.

Prediction: Smith-Njigba goes for 100 and two touchdowns.

2. Rashid Shaheed will be a factor in the backfield

Seattle debuted a Deebo Samuel-esque package against the Chargers, welcoming speedy wideout Rashid Shaheed to the backfield and using him like a running back. Shaheed scored on a toss against Los Angeles and looked like the explosive player Seattle paid him to be. With the Seahawks seemingly signing any running back they can get their hands on, expect to see Shaheed used more in key moments to generate explosives against a stout 49ers run defense that is holding teams to under 100 rushing yards per game.

Prediction: Shaheed goes for 50+ rushing yards.

3. Seahawks will cover -3

San Francisco, and especially quarterback Brock Purdy, have struggled against Mike Macdonald-led defenses for the last three years. The Seahawks defense held them to nine points, no touchdowns, in their last two meetings, and while nobody should expect that level of dominance on Sunday, it shouldn’t be far off. The 49ers are fresh off a battle with the Denver Broncos, who were missing several key players on defense, and only managed 24 points. Seattle will have to play more disciplined football than last week, but they should get the job done.

Prediction: Seahawks cover the three-point spread.

4. Game finishes with under 47.5 points

While Seattle should cover, this should be an old-fashioned rock fight, much like what these two teams put together in Week 18 of last season. Both of these offenses are battling through significant injuries and have not gotten off to the hottest starts. They will be forced to lean on their defenses and special teams to get this one done, which should result in a low-scoring and stressful game.

Prediction: Seahawks escape with a 21-17 victory, total points 38.

Closing thoughts

The Seahawks have been a frustrating team to watch in 2026, and that’s an unfortunate trend that should continue into this heated rivalry contest. While my confidence in the Dark Side defense is relatively high, as long as they can fix their penalty bug from last week, as they’ve looked the part through the first four games. Much depends on the health of Leonard Williams, however, Macdonald has earned enough trust for me to believe in his group.

Meanwhile, Seahawks’ offense has yet to face a defense as solid as San Francisco’s. Seattle will need a better performance from Darnold, especially in the turnover category, as this run game will likely struggle to get past Fred Warner.

This game will likely come down to the fourth quarter, so make sure to have your blood pressure medication of choice on hand Sunday at 1:25 p.m PT.

item.title: 5 plays that cost the Cowboys vs. the Buccaneers
item.description: What was the worst moment on Thursday night?
item.content:encoded:
Why? Just why? Why do the Dallas Cowboys keep disappointing this badly? You’re at home on a short week, playing a winless team that is starting an undrafted free agent at quarterback. You would have never noticed with how poorly the defense looked.

Once again, they failed to limit explosive plays. If the Tampa Bay Buccaneers wanted to gash them on the ground, they could. If they wanted to exploit them through the passing game, no problemo. This defense is a rudderless ship that cannot get out of its own way.

As for the offense that was tabbed the Greatest Offense There Is (GOTI), not so fast either. The offense led by Dak Prescott was lifeless in the first half. Prescott was far from his normal self, and the offense paid dearly for it.

When you lose this badly, and in this embarrassing way, there’s no shortage of identifying where it all went so sour. We’re going to sit on this loss for a while. Here are the key plays that cost the Cowboys. 

The drive that started it all, 1st QTR, 9:33, 3rd-and-4

The Cowboys were off to a fast start. After the receiving the opening kick, the Cowboys took a quick 7-0 lead and immediately put the pressure on Jalon Daniels and the offense to answer back. Facing an early 3rd-and-4, the Dallas defense does a good job in coverage, blanketing Tampa Bay’s available receivers.

However, Rashan Gary doesn’t keep containment on his side, and Daniels is able to escape the pocket to his right as he manages to get the first down running. This wiped away a 3-and-out opportunity. More than once, Gary failed to maintain the edge or make a tackle in space, and the Buccaneers benefited from it.

On Tampa Bay’s opening drive, the Buccaneers held the ball for 10:58 of game clock. During the drive, DaRon Bland drew a holding penalty. That nullified a sack and further kept the drive alive. That one play would have knocked the Buccaneers out of field goal range and ended an excruciating drive much sooner.

The Buccaneers more than doubled the time of possession in the first half versus the Cowboys. However, you can point back to Daniels getting out of the pocket initially to keep the chains moving and the Cowboys off the field, which foreshadowed a maddening evening. 

Dak misses a big shot to CeeDee Lamb, 2nd QTR 9:29, 3rd-and-10

If we know anything about Todd Bowles, he’s going to bring to bring pressure and overwhelm your offensive lineman with extra numbers in the face of the quarterback. Historically, Dak Prescott is very good against the blitz, but something wasn’t quite right with Prescott for much of the evening.

After a Bryan Anger punt that landed inside the Tampa Bay 5-yard line and a rare 3-and-out from the defense, the offense had prime real estate. The Cowboys had the chance to take back the lead and the momentum from the Buccaneers.

Facing a critical third down, Prescott breaks away from a sure sack and, once he bails the pocket, has a clear shot down the field at CeeDee Lamb. If Prescott lays the ball out and puts some air under it, Lamb likely makes the catch and waltzes into the end zone.

Instead, Prescott throws it short, and it is very nearly intercepted. Had Prescott hit that throw deep, it likely changes the way Bowles attacks the Dallas offense the remainder of the night. Prescott has been terrific all season, but that was one he had to have. There was a lid on the Cowboys offense for far too long on the evening and that moment they needed to have to get out of that funk. 

Bucky breaks free 3rd QTR 14:54, 1st-and-10

Take your pick of which explosive play allowed by the defense upset you the most. Was it the defense allowing a 3rd-and-21 to be converted after bailing out into a soft zone defense with easy access to Emeka Egbuka? Or was it DaRon Bland falling as Tez Johnson was wide open in the secondary and took it 64 yards?

Let’s settle on Bucky Irving’s 72-yard run to open the half. The Cowboys decided to aggressively blitz the run to stop Irving. For a moment, it looked to be successful. However, the defense didn’t show enough effort to rally to the ball to make the tackle.

It looks like Jaishawn Barham did a solid job redirecting Irving in the backfield, but instead Irving leaks out of the pile of bodies to set up Tampa Bay deep in Dallas territory. Still shell-shocked from what happened, the defense looks like they don’t know what hit them. On the very next play, Emeka Egbuka trots in for the score to give the Buccaneers the lead.

It’s an abysmal pattern, but this defense hemorrhages big plays at the worst possible time. 

Bland drops the ball, 4QTR 3:58, 3rd-and-8

DaRon Bland had a rough night. Multiple times he was on the receiving end of huge plays that went against his team. He hasn’t been playing very well for quite a long time, but all could have been forgiven if he just made one play that slipped through his fingers.

At this point in the game, the Cowboys should be disappointed with how they had played against Jalon Daniels. They hadn’t been able to get him to the ground regularly; they were unable to cover his receivers, and they had allowed him to overcome repeated penalties by his offense.

Yet, with the Cowboys needing to score a touchdown and a two-point conversion, Daniels threw a pass right to Bland that he should’ve intercepted for a touchdown. This is the same player that has the NFL record for most interceptions returned for a touchdown in a given season. If there was any indicator that Bland isn’t the player he once was and probably wont ever be again, its that moment right there.

There are few play calls by Christian Parker where you feel he got the better of the opposing offensive coordinator. Dallas missed his call of the night. Parker dialed up a blitz to ensure that Daniels would be forced to get the ball out quickly, and Bland also knew it and was in perfect position. That play call was worth six points, and Bland couldn’t deliver. 

Ferguson completes the hat trick 4th QTR 1:22

The Cowboys turned the ball over three times on Thursday night; two of them were because of balls that hit the intended receiver in the hands. Jake Ferguson’s mishandling of Dak Prescott’s pass resulted in effectively the game-sealing turnover, which left fans in attendance stunned.

For the second week in a row, Dak Prescott was engineering a late fourth-quarter drive. It looked as if he was going to get his sputtering offense in the end zone once again. At that point, the personnel was falling apart. Tyler Guyton had left the game; CeeDee Lamb was also on the sideline with a quad injury.

For as poorly as he had been playing, Prescott was doing his best to drag his offense to a tie. That is, until Jake Ferguson let the ball slip through his hands, off his helmet, and into the arms of Alex Anzalone.

In the last few weeks, Ferguson has mishandled the football several times. From a fumble in Brazil to a drop during the two-minute offense before the break, Ferguson had to come up with that catch at the end of regulation. It’s a shame that the game was ultimately decided by a simple pitch-and-catch that was poorly executed.

item.title: Hunting Explosives: Revisiting the Bears’ Big Plays from Week 4
item.description: Breaking down the Chicago Bears' explosive plays highlighted by Rome Odunze, Kyle Monangai, and Luther Burden.
item.content:encoded:
What, exactly, did I get myself into? Recap all the explosive plays each week, that won’t be that big of a deal. The Bears are starting a backup quarterback, it’ll probably be a light week.

Wrong.

Eleven explosive plays as the Bears offense was on the field for about three quarters of the game. Insane numbers put up all around, explosives included. Let’s get to it.

Explosive Play 4.1 – Q1 12:06, 3rd and 6 from the Chicago 26. Tyson Bagent passes short middle to Rome Odunze for 21 yards.

Right off the bat, the Bears come out in shotgun in a 2×2 formation. Rome and Loveland work together on the left. Loveland’s route, for some reason, draws the attention of both Jets defenders, allowing Rome to run right by both into an empty pocket in the secondary. Bagent delivers a quick ball and just like that, the first explosive of the day. This sure seems like a blown coverage but excellent job of finding it quickly and delivering a good ball.

Explosive Play 4.2 – Q1 11:38, 1st and 10 from the Chicago 47. Tyson Bagent passes complete deep middle to Luther Burden for 20 yards.

On the very next play, Bagent goes back under center. Loveland motions right to left where Cole Kmet is attached next to Theo Benedet. Bagent gives a play action fake to Monangai before firing over the middle to Burden for back to back explosive passes. This is a bit more impressive here delivering a ball up and over the second level to Burden before the safety can make a play on it. Excellent opening sequence.

Explosive Play 4.3 – Q1 6:20, 2nd and 8 from the Chicago 45. Tyson Bagent completes pass deep right to Luther Burden for 22 yards.

Back in shotgun here with 12 personnel on the field (Loveland and Kmet). Burden works from the left of the formation, Rome from the right. Burden and Rome run a deep crossing concept with the deep safety moving with Rome. Burden has a step on his defender and Bagent puts a decent ball on him as Luther tries to turn it up to an even bigger play. Great concept, read out well by Bagent, executed all around.

Explosive Play 4.4 – Q1 2:57, 4th and 1 from the Jets 21. D’Andre Swift runs off right end for 13 yards.

Rolling out the 13 personnel here with Roush and Kmet attached on the left side of the line and Loveland motioning left to right, Bagent pitches to Swift on the short side of the field on this fourth down call. The Jets flow to the pitch well – don’t get me wrong, Swift is going to pick this up 10/10 times as blocked – but the cut back here is beautiful to make this an explosive carry. While Ben Johnson would say all play calls are designed to go for an explosive, you need one here and Swift’s agility and vision makes it into a big play.

Drive capper (finally) here by Monangai on 4th and goal. Jets defense was stout on the goal line early, but this was a nice breakthrough.

Explosive Play 4.5 – Q2 8:09, 1st and 10 from the Chicago 29. Kyle Monangai runs off right end for 19 yards.

Bread and butter. The Bears come out in 12 personnel here with Kmet and Loveland attached to the right side of the formation next to Darnell Wright and Jonah Jackson. Burden motions right to left and Monangai takes the handoff and works behind the strength of the Bears offense. Wright and Kmet double the defensive end before Kmet quickly works to the second level. Jonah has no problem with the defensive tackle and Thuney executes a nice reach block on the back side of the play with help of a quick stab from Bradbury before he works to the second level. Monangai heads in the direction between Wright and Loveland’s blocks but as the safety commits to his run fit to the outside, Monangai cuts back up the middle and finds a patch of Bermuda grass. The backside linebacker makes the play well down the field. The Bears are so good at these run concepts and running to that side of the line.

Explosive Play 4.6 – Q2 0:27, 3rd and 5 from the Chicago 47. Tyson Bagent completes pass deep middle to Rome Odunze for 37 yards.

This drive was just about dead. Bears come out with three receivers bunched to the right side with Loveland attached on the left. Raymond draws the attention of two Jets defenders running to the boundary, allowing Rome to work one on one. This is just Rome winning beating the safety with some route running savvy at the top of the route and Bagent with the patience to find him. Excellent pocket from the offensive line allows the patience, which leads to three points at the end of the half.

Explosive Play 4.7 – Q3 9:51, 1st and 10 from the Chicago 4. Tyson Bagent completes pass deep left to Rome Odunze for 20 yards.

This is a really good route by Rome and nice composure from Bagent delivering a good ball while standing in the end zone. The Bears use 12 personnel with Kmet and Loveland attached to the right. They’re at the four yard line. This is obviously a run to the right side to get a little breathing room, right?

Wrong. Play action, trust your blocking, and Bagent delivers in rhythm. Rome does everything incredibly well here, including the one-handed grab to finish. This led a long drive that ended with a second Monangai score. Our friend Jacob Infante with the note on Rome’s route:

Explosive Play 4.8 – Q3 0:21, 1st and 1o from the Chicago 34. Luther Burden runs around left end for 11 yards.

This is a very fun drive if you like the run game. The Bears use 11 personnel with Roush attached to Wright on the right side. Burden is motioned from right to left and gets the ball on a jet sweep while the line and fake to the back commits the blocking to the right. The Jets all bite on the run action except for one Jets defender who has no chance at the speedy Burden. The receivers do a nice job maintaining their blocks on the left side of the field and Burden has a first down before he’s touched.

Explosive Play 4.9 – Q4 15:00, 1st and 10 from the Chicago 45. Kyle Monangai runs over left end for 11 yards.

Next play, the Bears come out to start the 4th quarter in 13 personnel with Loveland and Kmet lined up to the left side of the line with Roush starting on the right and motioning over to the strength of the formation. Bagent hands to Monangai on an outside zone play and the Bears simply have numbers. Hat on a hat gives Monangai a clear runway before first contact five yards down field. Three Jets defenders converge but he bursts through for an additional six yards after contact. He’s truly amazing with a head of steam. Scheme and blocking got him a positive gain of five and the explosive run style of Monangai earns the extra six.

Explosive Play 4.10 – Q4 14:12, 2nd and 10 from the Jets 44. Kyle Monangai runs over right guard for 26 yards.

Two plays later. the Bears use Kmet as a fullback in a traditional I-Formation. Burden motions right to left and Monangai takes the handoff and follows Kmet to the right. Bradbury is getting walked back here by the defensive tackle but he doesn’t disengage in time and Monangai runs right by him. The guards both work to the second level beautifully and take the linebackers out of the play. Monangai finds the opening and bursts through, makes a move on the safety, then viciously stiff arms a Jets defender before dragging two Jets defenders for even more yardage. Incredible impressive run absolutely beating down a tired defense.

Explosive Play 4.11 – Q4 12:52, 2nd and 7 from the Jets 15. Roschon Johnson runs over left guard for 11 yards.

Oh, you want a third explosive run on one drive? Well, here you go. Bears use 13 personnel with Roschon Johnson getting a chance to carry the pill. All three tight ends align to the right side of the formation with Rome the lone receiver on the left. RoJo starts right but finds the cutback near the line of scrimmage with green grass. The cutback earns him nine yards before contact before carrying two Jets defenders for another Chicago Bears first down and the eleventh and final explosive play of the game.

2026 Explosive Play Count: Kyle Monangai 7, D’Andre Swift 6, Rome Odunze 6, Luther Burden 5, Caleb Williams 4, Kalif Raymond 2, and one each for Cole Kmet and Roschon Johnson.

What was your favorite explosive play from this one? For me, it’s the strike to Rome for 37 at the end of the half. Impressive all around.

item.title: Browns Week 5: Jets rule out 3 starters early on Friday
item.description: The Cleveland Browns will not have to face 3 offensive starters for the New York Jets including Breece Hall, AD Mitchell
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns head into their Week 5 matchup with the New York Jets with injury concerns, especially on the defensive line. With fans feeling more confident and some worried about a trap game, injuries tend to be a huge story throughout most of the NFL season, and this week will be no different.

The home Jets have had their own injury issues with four players sitting out the first two practices of the week, including RB Breece Hall, OL Dylan Parham, and WR Adonai Mitchell. With New York playing better, but still sitting with a 1-3 record, Week 5 just got more difficult for the green and white:

Hall, Parham, and Mitchell are all starters for the Jets offense.

Hall leads the team in rushing with 163 yards, despite only playing three games. His backup, Braelon Allen, has just 120 yards in four contests. Mitchell is New York’s big play receiver, leading the team with a 13.7 yards-per-catch average and is fourth on the team with 123 yards receiving.

According to the Jets’ unofficial depth chart, Jordan Meredith will start in Parham’s place. Meredith has started 21 games in his five-year career after going undrafted out of Western Kentucky.

WRs Malik McClain, Isaiah Williams, and Jamaal Pritchett fill out the depth chart behind star WR Garrett Wilson. Of the three backups, only Williams has caught a pass this year, 10 for 135 yards and a touchdown.

item.title: Fantasy Football Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Justin Boone's lineup advice for Week 5
item.description: Justin Boone gets those lineups in shape for Week 5 fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
Make any day feel like Game Day with the Burger King Game Day Menu. Before you take your first bite, get your lineup ready with this week's must-starts and sits.

Justin Boone provides a weekly look at undervalued fantasy players to consider starting this week and potential busts you might want to leave on your bench. 

For the rest of your lineup decisions, consult his Week 5 rankings. 

Starts

Matthew Stafford, QB, Rams

vs. Bills

Stafford's fantasy numbers have been a mixed bag in the opening month, with two weeks as a top-10 QB and two finishes outside the top 25. Fortunately, his next matchup has the makings for one of the best prime-time shootouts of the season. 

The Rams will host the Bills on Monday Night Football, in a game tied for the highest projected point total on the week at 54.5.

Buffalo is allowing the fourth-most fantasy points to opposing passers, including a QB1 overall result to Drake Maye last week. 

Other QBs to start:

  • Drake Maye vs. Raiders – Speaking of Maye, he finally looked more like his 2025 self in Week 4. The most exciting outcome was his season-highs in carries (8) and rushing yards (54), which Mike Vrabel highlighted as a key to their victory. If Maye keeps it up, he'll return to high-end fantasy QB1 territory. 

  • Jared Goff at Cardinals – Goff might not be at home for this one, but this is a dome game with a 54.5 projected point total against an Arizona defense that's giving up the fifth-most fantasy points to QBs.

Jaylen Warren, RB, Steelers

vs. Colts

With Rico Dowdle sitting out the last couple of games due to a toe injury, Warren has made the most of his increased workload. Despite not finding the end zone in either contest, he still racked up 302 scrimmage yards and six receptions on 44 touches during those two weeks. 

Dowdle is practicing on a limited basis so far this week and may return to the lineup, but Warren remains a strong start either way after showcasing his potential recently. 

The Colts are also the eighth-best matchup for fantasy RBs, which is by far his easiest opponent through the first five weeks. You can confidently start Warren once again whether Dowdle is active or not. 

Other RBs to start:

  • Bhayshul Tuten vs. Eagles (London) – Tuten was one of my recommended buys this week, since he's been so close to much bigger stat lines recently. He's RB16 on the year, topping 85 scrimmage yards in three of his four games and is coming off season-highs in usage. He also had two TDs called back due to penalties last week. He should see plenty of work with the Jags heavily favored over the banged-up Eagles. 

  • Emanuel Wilson vs. 49ers – Wilson is coming off a 120-yard, two-touchdown effort and facing a 49ers defense that's let four different backs reach double-digit fantasy points against them in four weeks. Seattle also ran all over San Francisco in its matchups last season. 

  • Braelon Allen vs. Browns – It's hard to judge the Jets offense based on their performance in Week 4, since the Bears completely controlled the game and time of possession. Even so, Allen finished with 16 touches, including all 14 of New York's rushing attempts. I like his chances against a Browns defense allowing 103.5 scrimmage yards per game to starting RBs this season. 

Jameson Williams, WR, Lions

at Cardinals

Williams was highlighted as a start last week in this space and answered the call with six receptions and 102 yards on eight targets. Is it risky to go back to the well expecting another spike week from the volatile WR3? Yes, but fantasy managers should feel good about his outlook once again. 

In addition to being projected as a high-scoring affair in the desert, Williams also gets to face a generous Cardinals defense. Arizona is the fourth-friendliest fantasy opponent for wideouts and has given up a league-leading 11 receiving TDs. 

Other WRs to start:

  • DK Metcalf vs. Colts – With Michael Pittman Jr. sidelined with a foot injury, Metcalf will be asked to carry the passing game. His nine targets in Week 4 are a promising sign of things to come and resulted in a 5-115-0 stat line versus the Browns. Indy is not a matchup to be feared. 

  • Romeo Doubs vs. Raiders – With A.J. Brown and now Mack Hollins injured, Doubs has become the focal point of New England's passing attack. Over the last three weeks, he's delivered solid numbers with 96 yards, 49 yards and then his six-catch, 58-yard, two-touchdown explosion in Week 4. The nine targets in that game are what I find the most alluring. Expect Doubs to be featured against a Raiders defense that's permitted 100-yard games to wideouts in back-to-back weeks. 

  • Dohnte Meyers at Dolphins – Tee Higgins seems unlikely to play in Week 5 and Ja'Marr Chase is in a race to be cleared from concussion protocol before Sunday. That puts Meyers in position to start, after his seven-catch, 82-yard performance last week. If Chase sits out as well, Meyers will be a high-end fantasy WR3 with upside. If Chase plays, Meyers can still be started as a WR3/flex. 

Mike Gesicki, TE, Bengals

at Dolphins

We can stick with the Bengals when searching for a tight end to start this week. With Chase still working to get cleared and Higgins seeming more doubtful by the day, Gesicki is firmly in play for fantasy. 

He's been a sneaky starter most weeks in the opening month, with touchdowns in three of his four outings. Now, he's set to benefit from the receiver injuries and see increased volume against his old team, the Dolphins. 

Miami is the fifth-best matchup for fantasy tight ends, allowing George Kittle (80 yards, TD), Travis Kelce (59 yards, TD) and T.J. Hockenson (119 yards) to have big days against them over the past three weeks. 

Other TEs to start:

  • Juwan Johnson vs. Vikings – Suggesting players to start against Minnesota's defense doesn't come without risk. However, the Vikings have given up at least 50 yards to a tight end three times in four weeks and Johnson has posted at least 50 yards in every game. He also has three touchdowns on the season. 

  • Tyler Higbee vs. Bills – With Terrance Ferguson sidelined, Higbee has found the fountain of youth, with 8-62-1 and 5-67-0 stat lines in the last two games. He's worthy of consideration as a streaming option in a potentially high-scoring MNF matchup with the Bills, who are still figuring things out under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. 

Sits

Jalen Hurts, QB, Eagles

vs. Jaguars (London)

They say things can always get worse, but the Eagles are putting that to the test at the moment. 

DeVonta Smith and Saquon Barkley are sidelined, while Dallas Goedert is trying to return from injury after a two-game absence. Wideout Dontayvion Wicks also popped up on the injury report with a new hamstring injury and a limited practice on Thursday.

To make matters worse, the offensive line is in complete disarray following the sudden retirement of Lane Johnson, the trade of Cam Jurgens and a cavalcade of injuries, including Landon Dickerson, Fred Johnson and Drew Kendall. 

Now, they're traveling to London to face a Jaguars defense that's known for shutting down the run, but has also been tough on QBs this year. This is not the time to have Hurts in your lineup. 

Other QBs to sit:

  • Sam Darnold vs. 49ers – San Francisco is allowing the seventh-fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks in 2026. The Niners also held Darnold in check during their three meetings last season in Week 1 (150 yards, no TDs), Week 18 (198 yards, no TDs) and the divisional round (124 yards, TD).

  • Justin Herbert vs. Broncos – Herbert has played so poorly this year (QB22, QB24, QB23, QB27) that he's not even worth starting against a Broncos defense that will be without starting corners Patrick Surtain II and Riley Moss. 

Alvin Kamara, RB, Saints

vs. Vikings

While it might not have looked pretty at times, Kamara came through for fantasy managers in Week 4 with seven carries for 23 yards, five catches for 35 yards and two touchdowns on Monday Night Football. 

Hopefully no one is talking themselves into Kamara being a strong fantasy option after that game. Even with Travis Etienne Jr. on IR, Kamara still only played 38% of the snaps — sharing the load with Kendre Miller and CJ Donaldson. 

Brian Flores' defense isn't going to make life easy on him, either. Prior to Ollie Gordon II's somewhat flukey 100-yard, one-touchdown stat line on just nine carries, the Vikings had held every back they'd faced under 50 rushing yards. On paper, Minnesota is the toughest opponent for fantasy backs in 2026. The 31-year-old Kamara remains a desperation TD-or-bust RB3, who may have trouble holding up to these workloads. 

Other RBs to sit:

  • Omarion Hampton vs. Broncos – Hampton's usage is trending in the wrong direction after he split snaps almost evenly with Keaton Mitchell and Kimani Vidal last week. He's managed to salvage his fantasy weeks by scoring touchdowns in three of four games so far, but that won't always be the case. Follow the volume, which led to a season-low 11 touches in Week 4.

  • Tony Pollard vs. Texans – Pollard has come through with a couple usable stat lines lately, but he's still a risky RB3 with limited scoring upside. Though the Texans defense might not be as ferocious as it was in 2025, I would still be avoiding Pollard in this matchup. 

  • J.K. Dobbins at Chargers – Dobbins has been held under 50 rushing in every game this season, has a very limited role in the passing game and hasn't found the end zone. Even a revenge game narrative against the Chargers isn't enough to convince me to start him. 

Devaughn Vele, WR, Saints

vs. Vikings

Vele has been an outstanding fantasy pickup in the opening month, with at least 50 yards in three of his games and a pair of touchdowns. 

Coming off a primetime contest where many people watched him catch six passes for 54 yards and a score, fantasy managers might be getting comfortable starting him. I'd advise against it this week. 

The Vikings are a challenging defense and Vele has benefitted from some easier matchups in the first four weeks. His only tougher opponent was the Raiders (eighth-fewest fantasy points to WRs), who held him to just three catches for 39 yards. You don't have to drop Vele until Jordyn Tyson returns, just lower your expectations against more difficult opponents like Minnesota. 

Other WRs to sit

  • Eagles WRs vs. Jaguars (London) – This probably goes without saying, but you shouldn't be mining for value on the Eagles' WR depth chart right now. We'll monitor Dontayvion Wicks's status after he showed up with a new injury on Thursday and Makai Lemon remains a deeper stash for later in the season. You just can't trust any of Philly's wideouts in your lineup right now with all the injuries and struggles this offense is dealing with. 

  • Courtland Sutton at Chargers – Sutton has only topped 25 yards in one game this season and is fresh off a one-catch, four-yard effort against the 49ers. Even with Pat Bryant potentially missing time due to injury, Sutton isn't someone I'm willing to put in lineups. Troy Franklin and Marvin Mims Jr. will simply see more work in Bryant's absence. 

  • Wan'Dale Robinson vs. Texans – Robinson has found the end zone in consecutive weeks, but don't get used to it. This is a receiver who hasn't scored more than four touchdowns in an NFL season. He's a low-floor, low-ceiling WR4/flex. 

T.J. Hockenson, TE, Vikings

at Saints

After missing last week with an ankle injury, Justin Jefferson has practiced in a limited fashion so far this week. That makes it seem like he's trending in the right direction to play, but remember the Vikings have a Week 6 bye. So, if Minnesota wants to play it safe with the star wideout, he could sit again. 

If Jefferson plays, Hockenson goes back to being a low-end TE2 who doesn't qualify as a fantasy starter. However, even if Jefferson is ruled out, fantasy managers should be cautious about chasing Hockenson's 13-catch, 119-yard stat line from last week. 

Remember when Dalton Schultz had a 12-catch, 140-yard game for the Texans when Nico Collins was sidelined? Collins remained out the next week, but Schultz drew more defensive attention and flopped with just three catches and 30 yards. Hockenson is in a similar group at the position, making him just a risky streamer.  

Other TEs to sit:

  • Dalton Schultz at Titans – Aside from that one big blowup game, Schultz has been kept to 35 yards or less in his three other appearances. That includes just two grabs for nine yards last week. 

  • Kyle Pitts Sr. vs. Ravens – Don't be tempted by Pitts' 47-yard outing last week. It came on just three catches, while running a route on just 43% of the Falcons' dropbacks. He's well off the fantasy radar and should be dropped in most redraft leagues.

item.title: Fantasy Football: 3 players set to enter the Circle of Trust in Week 5 — and 3 who could fall out
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen highlights six players moving in opposite directions heading into Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
Let me know if this feels familiar to you. I work with all sorts of people at my day job. From engineers like myself with varying fields of expertise, to contracting, finance or mission support, the list of groups and job titles goes on forever. The use of buzzwords like "cross-functional" and "multi-disciplinary" is frequent, to say the least. And I interface (another one!) with folks from each group almost daily. 

But when I need stuff done, I've got my people. The few I can ping on Teams, give them a quick rundown of the context or need, and I've got an answer in my inbox mere hours later.

We have guys like that in fantasy football.

Some are easy to spot because of their ADP. Others have worked their way onto the edge of our circle of trust. And if things break right (or don't) in Week 5, these could be our go-to options for the rest of the season.

Almost in the circle

Trevor Lawrence, QB, Jaguars

I'll admit that listing Trevor Lawrence as a guy fantasy managers would be right not to trust fully feels wrong. As far as ethical passers go, Duval has one of the best. 

Trevor Lawrence: Over the Middle

- 33/41 (80.5%)
- 414 Yards
- 6 TDs 1 INT
- 138.16 NFL

Data: @SumerSportspic.twitter.com/QKWUR6OPj6

— Daniel Griffis (@DanDGriffis) October 6, 2026

I was (way up) in the stands as Lawrence led drive after drive against my Bengals in Week 4. And there were only three series where I thought Cincinnati had a chance to come back. His buy-in and understanding of HC Liam Coen's scheme look much improved from '25. There are no efficiency rankings where you won't find Lawrence inside the top 12. But just because he's passing well doesn't mean he's doing it often.

  • Week 1: -4.3% (PROE), 20th (Rank) 

  • Week 2: -3.3%, 22nd 

  • Week 3: -2.5%, 23rd 

  • Week 4: -2.0%, 18th 

Through four weeks, Lawrence's 28.5 dropbacks per game rank 28th among all starters. Cam Ward has more red-zone dropbacks per game than Lawrence. His rushing rate is also down as he's seen fewer pressures each week. As a result, Lawrence has been a great real-life QB, but mediocre for fantasy. But there's a path for him to stay on our good side this weekend.

Philadelphia's defense isn't the same vaunted unit from years past. They're 18th in passing yards per game allowed and below the league average in defensive EPA per play. The only mobile QB the Eagles have faced was Jayden Daniels, and his 31 rushing yards give Lawrence a low floor for boosting his output. With another strong outing in Week 5, and a stretch of favorable matchups ahead, we should have more confidence about Lawrence moving forward.

Aaron Jones Sr., RB, Vikings

To be clear, I don't think the problem is Aaron Jones Sr.

Plenty of Aaron Jones YAC 📈

MIAvsMIN on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/gsDeZcDj0o

— NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026

It's been three weeks since Jordan Mason went on injured reserve. We expected the touches to condense around the 31-year-old RB. And so far, that part of the equation has worked in our favor.

  • Rush Att. Share (w/out Mason): 81%, 5th (among all RBs – min. 75 snaps)

  • Route Rate: 55%, 8th 

  • Target Share: 17%, 4th 

Few other RBs are getting the same amount of work as Jones. His 23 touches per game are more than Jahmyr Gibbs (22.7), Kyren Williams (20.3) and James Cook (20). Jones has run 56 routes in three weeks. Ashton Jeanty has 55 carries. The usage couldn't be better. His offense could be, though.

Kyler Murray Throws This Pass Away 😭

It’s Been A Tough Half Against The Worst Team In The League. pic.twitter.com/5nvCpNosX4

— SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) October 4, 2026

I realize that tweet only shows one rep. But it highlights a larger trend regarding the early returns of the Kyler Murray experience. When Carson Wentz started in place of Murray, the offense operated on time, with Wentz averaging 2.53 seconds per pass. Not only is Murray getting the ball out at that same pace on just 40.9% of his throws, but they're only traveling 2.7 air yards. He's tied for the eighth-fewest attempts to the intermediate part of the field. But they've got another shot to change up on Sunday.

New Orleans has surrendered the most PPG to RBs to date. That'll give Jones a better path to rushing production and more manageable down-and-distance for Murray in obvious passing situations — the ideal setup right before the Vikings head into their bye.

Isaiah Likely, TE, Giants

After starting off the season as the TE1, Isaiah Likely faded into replacement level after Jaxson Dart went down. Plus, playing with Jameis Winston, at least at times, hasn't looked like the boon we thought it'd be.

Jameis Winston throws another interception despite Isaiah Likely being wide open pic.twitter.com/YvWjVtXxyZ

— Talkin’ Giants (@TalkinGiants) October 4, 2026

Watching a QB throw a meatball sub to the defense while your receiver stands alone is one of the most demoralizing things to watch as a fantasy gamer. It's even worse for TEs, as their target share relative to WRs is lower. However, as I noted in my offseason TE strategy piece, finding the guys cosplaying as receivers should be our first step. And even as Winston has continued to warm up, Likely has maintained his role as the second option in the offense.

  • Route Rate (Weeks 3-4): 90%, 4th (among all TEs – min. 40 routes)

  • Targets per Route Run: 32%, 1st 

  • Target Share: 34%, 1st 

It's not like Malachi Fields' or Darnell Mooney's on-field play has earned them more attention. The offense still flows through the same two pass-catchers. Even better, Winston's CPOE has picked up across his two full starts (Week 3: 4.8%, Week 4: +1.3%). And going against a defense allowing the fourth-most points to his position on Sunday, Likely should be back in the TE1 discussion after Week 5.

Teetering on the Edge

Jalen Hurts, QB Eagles

Our perception of the Eagles has completely flipped since the end of Week 4. Multiple pass-catchers are still hurt (with Dontayvion Wicks now included). The elite offensive line is no more. And yet, Jalen Hurts has been trying to make plays.

DARIUS COOPER JUST TURNED A JALEN HURTS PICK INTO A TOUCHDOWN 🔥pic.twitter.com/S3QTHCHDWL

— Yahoo Fantasy Sports (@YahooFantasy) October 4, 2026

OK, let me add in the necessary context here. Sure, Hurts had his third multi-TD game against the Rams. But he only threw for 93 yards. Surprisingly, he's the third QB this season to start and finish a game and amass less than 100 through the air. But remember, passers with early-round price tags need throwing efficiency and a boost via rushing to pay off their ADP. Neither has been there through the first month.

  • Passing Success Rate: 37.3%, 27th (among all starters)

  • EPA per Dropback: -0.08, 24th 

  • Pressure-to-Sack Ratio: 20.0%, 24th 

The real head-scratcher has been the decline in rushing. Hurts' designed rushing rate is almost a third of what it was at this point last year (16.6% to 6.8%). The scrambling is also down. Instead, drive-killing sacks are on the rise. And against a Jacksonville defense that just clocked Joe Burrow 11 times, managers should already have another QB on their bench should Hurts disappoint again.

Jaylen Waddle, WR, Broncos

I saw the post below and had to confirm the caption. But honestly, this is why Waddle should be tumbling down the rest-of-season ranks.

JAYLEN WADDLE SCORES HIS FIRST TOUCHDOWN AS A BRONCO 🔥

(via: @Broncos) pic.twitter.com/0wemrqHFYk

— The Sporting News (@sportingnews) October 4, 2026

We're a month into the season. Bo Nix has completed five touchdown passes. That's bad enough! Sam Darnold has thrown for six scores, and he (effectively) missed two games. Anyway, taking this long to connect with Nix's supposed WR1 in the end zone is already a yellow flag. The other is Waddle's place within the passing game.

  • Target Share: 22%

  • Route Rate: 78%

  • Snap Share: 68%

Waddle has the third-highest snap rate of the Broncos' WRs when they use heavy-personnel packages. His four (!) red-zone targets might be second-most on the team, but Week 4 was the first look with a depth of double digits. In fact, Nix is yet to throw a pass to Waddle when he's been in the end zone.

The combination of taking on the Chargers' defense and HC Sean Payton resuming play-calling duties might be all it takes. But without a significant shift in opportunities and results, Waddle may fall into the WR3 category for the rest of the season.

Dalton Kincaid, TE, Bills

I, too, believed in Dalton Kincaid's return to stardom. He was the TE5 and TE3 to start the season. And touchdowns weren't propping up the results. The YAC was back, along with a healthy workload. But now, we're clinging to coachspeak for optimism. 

Brady says Kincaid's two targets were too few and he needs to get him the ball more

Joe Brady: “There's no reason Dalton Kincaid should have two targets, especially with the flow of the game and how that goes. I gotta find a way to get the ball in his hands and do a better job… pic.twitter.com/CcckgPKyZQ

— MicNuggets (@micnuggetsnfl) October 4, 2026

However, let's go back to our Likely discussion. The logic train was that a change in on-field deployment would be the signal. Of course, we'd like to see a consistent flow of attempts. But for TEs especially, cardio is the path to staying involved in the offense. And that hasn't changed too much for Kincaid.

  • Route Rate: 68.6% (Weeks 1-2), 60.6% (Weeks 3-4)

  • Snap Share: 71.9%, 62.4%

  • Slot Rate: 31.0%, 38.4%

No, HC Joe Brady isn't asking Kincaid to block more. PFF's charting had him with five pass-blocking snaps in the first two weeks and just two across Weeks 3 and 4. Also, no, Dawson Knox isn't playing more. He's running a similar number of routes and getting one or two targets per game, like always. Said another way, in most situations, we'd look for a regression to what we saw to start the season. 

DJ Moore's (likely) absence will condense Josh Allen's target tree, opening up more work for Kincaid. But Keon Coleman is looking like the receiver the Bills drafted. And Khalil Shakir continues to reset downs when Allen needs them most. Unless we can see a concerted effort to make Kincaid a focal point of the passing game, his TE1 status will be in jeopardy.

item.title: Award-winning season loading for Browns rookie, according to ESPN
item.description: The Cleveland Browns 2026 NFL Draft is coming along great, which could lead to Denzel Boston winning OROY.
item.content:encoded:
Fans of the Cleveland Browns were very excited when GM Andrew Berry brought in two wide receivers early in the 2026 NFL Draft. Almost no one could have imagined, at that time, that the Browns would be 3-1 after a very rough start in Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season. Cleveland’s offense has gone from terrible in 2025 to a passing grade in 2026.

HC Todd Monken gets a lot of credit for that, but Berry’s additions have been huge. WRs KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston are starting and making an impact, while OLmen Spencer Fano and Austin Barber are doing the same upfront.

According to ESPN’s Bill Barnwell, Boston’s season has put him on track to be the NFL’s Offensive Rookie of the Year:

Boston announced his presence in Week 1 with a 46-yard catch on a post route in garbage time, running past Jags cornerback Montaric Brown for his first pro touchdown. Boston has continued to make plays downfield, with catches of 28, 55 and 60 yards over his first four games. He and Zay Flowers are the only two NFL wide receivers with three catches of 45 yards or more through the first four weeks of the 2026 season.

In a league where teams are desperate for deep threats, Boston ranks fourth in air yards per target (16.9) while bringing in nearly 60% of the passes thrown in his direction. He’s already enough of a downfield burner to give opposing defenses serious pause, and Boston has been one of the biggest reasons the Browns have been surprisingly effective on offense this season.

The 6’4” Washington product has shown the ability to win on routes in multiple ways. His size allows him to box out defenders and break tackles, while his speed and quickness have helped him separate and run away from opponents. In four games, Boston has 13 receptions for 284 yards and two touchdowns.

To put that in perspective, only two receivers (Jerry Jeudy, Isaiah Bond) had more receiving yards all of last season. Boston is well on his way to eclipsing the team’s leading pass catcher, TE Harold Fannin Jr., from last season as well (731 yards).

Cleveland’s roster already includes the last two Defensive Rookies of the Year in DE Jared Verse and LB Carson Schwesinger; Boston could keep that streak going with another award-winning season.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 5 Fades & Busts: Jalen Hurts is officially out of the top 12
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Matt Okada fades some startable players in Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the fifth of 17 weekly articles spotlighting the fantasy fades of the week! I am your host, Matt Okada, and I'll be bringing you half a dozen potential busts each and every Friday, from now until fantasy championships.

As a note, just because a player earns a "fade" or "bust" designation doesn't automatically mean they should be benched — it depends on the rest of your roster or the options on your waiver wire. But you can expect them to fall short of expectations (when I get them right). I include a "What to Do" section for every player to help with that.

Without further ado, here is my list for Week 5 of the 2026 season.

Jalen Hurts, QB, Eagles at Jaguars

Jalen Hurts' name and Jalen Hurts' recent production simply do not occupy the same tier anymore. He's scored progressively fewer fantasy points each week this season, from 24.72 in Week 1 down to 13.62 and 13.52, respectively, the last two weeks.

Why?

A variety of reasons, but probably the biggest one is the decline in his rushing production. From 2021 through 2024, Jalen Hurts averaged 9.5 fantasy points per game as a rusher, comfortably the most by any quarterback. But since the start of last season, that average has dropped by 44%, as Hurts has rushed for just 26 yards per game over that span and has scored just once on the ground over his last nine starts. And unfortunately, he's not compensating as a passer in 2026, with just 178.3 passing yards per game.

After dicing up the Commanders in Week 1 — which doesn't carry all that much weight given how their defense has played — Hurts has thrown four touchdowns and three interceptions in the three games since. Now he enters a matchup with the Jaguars, who held Drake Maye, Bo Nix and Deshaun Watson outside the top-18 fantasy quarterbacks in each of their respective matchups. The Jags have allowed just three touchdown passes and snagged six interceptions through the first month, the best TD-INT ratio by any defense so far. While Hurts might still feel like a top-end QB1, the data does not support that feeling this season or this week. 

What to do ❓ As crazy as it might seem, Hurts is outside the top-12 quarterbacks for Week 5 and can absolutely be benched for streamers like Jacoby Brissett, Jameis Winston, C.J. Stroud and others.

David Montgomery, RB, Texans at Titans

Speaking of players whose elite fantasy history and current fantasy output don't match up ... David Montgomery has been awful. He unfortunately fooled fantasy managers with a 28.9-point, three-touchdown performance in Week 1, but has since been a major disappointment. Over the last three contests, he's averaged just 4.5 fantasy points and 22.3 rushing yards per game. He hasn't had more than 60 rushing yards in a game all year (even including Week 1). Since Week 2, he sports the position's second-fewest yards per carry (2.7), lowest success rate (23.4%) and lowest explosive run rate (2.1%). He's losing snaps and drives to Woody Marks and appears to be entirely touchdown-dependent for fantasy.

If Houston doesn't find its way into the red zone several times in a game, there appears to be absolutely no ceiling (or floor, frankly) for Montgomery. The Titans aren't exactly a standout matchup one way or another, though they've allowed the seventh-fewest yards per carry to running backs, so this is more of a PSA for fantasy managers still riding the high of opening weekend. Montgomery is borderline unplayable right now, and we need to adjust accordingly.

What to do ❓ I know running back looks incredibly shallow right now, but the fact that Montgomery is still outside RB2 range in that context should tell you everything you need to know. You're better off starting a replacement back like Braelon Allen or Emanuel Wilson, or a committee back like Kyle Monangai (or RJ Harvey in any form of PPR).

Jacory Croskey-Merritt, RB, Commanders vs. Giants

Jacory Croskey-Merritt is sort of a lesser version of Montgomery. He had a decent Week 1 — 63 rushing yards and a touchdown — but has averaged just 5.4 fantasy points per game since, with fewer than 45 rushing yards in all contests and zero touchdowns since Week 1. He's also been horribly inefficient, ranking bottom 10 among qualified running backs in success rate, EPA per carry, missed tackle rate and explosive run rate. Possibly as a result or due to Rachaad White's injury, the Commanders signed Austin Ekeler before Week 4. It’s bad news for JCM either way.

The veteran immediately outproduced Croskey-Merritt in the ground game — on far fewer carries and snaps — and seems like a major threat to the younger back's role and upside in the offense. As with the Titans against Montgomery, the Giants aren't a difficult matchup, but it doesn't particularly matter in this case. Neither the volume nor the efficiency for Croskey-Merritt offers any confidence in his floor or ceiling.

What to do ❓ Unfortunately for those who drafted "Bill" in the middle rounds hoping for a value RB2, he simply cannot be played except in the most dire of circumstances. Consider him a low-end FLEX at best.

Courtland Sutton, WR, Broncos at Chargers

I'll admit off the rip, Courtland Sutton has been so ineffective for fantasy that this "Fade" should be unnecessary, and some of you will probably question his inclusion at all. However, with Sutton still rostered in 70% of Yahoo leagues and Pat Bryant likely to miss Sunday's game against the Chargers, there will be a surprising number of fantasy managers tempted to slot Sutton into their lineup for one last shot at redemption.

Don't do it.

Through four games, Sutton has already had a 17.6% target share, second on the team to Jaylen Waddle's 20.8%, well ahead of Bryant's 9.6%. Bryant has stood out for fantasy because he's averaged 11.1 yards per target, with a 75.0% catch rate and a touchdown, but he's only seen 12 targets in total. Meanwhile, Sutton has been abysmal with his volume, averaging 3.9 yards per target with a 40.9% catch rate, both the worst marks by any player with 20+ targets in the entire league. Even if you gifted Bryant's three targets per game entirely to Sutton, at his rate of 0.6 half-PPR fantasy points per target, that would equate to a boost of just 1.8 fantasy points. As with the running backs above, the Chargers are actually a soft matchup for wide receivers, but it just doesn't matter with the way Sutton is playing this season. Frankly, if he doesn't prove me wrong with a vintage game this week, he's probably going to be droppable come the Week 6 waiver run.

What to do ❓ Do not start Sutton under basically any circumstance. Even in deeper leagues or on rosters with extra WR slots, I'd rather play guys like Kalif Raymond, Wan'Dale Robinson, Tre' Harris in the same game or even waiver wire adds Keon Coleman and Dohnte Meyers.

Josh Downs, WR, Colts at Steelers

Disclaimer: I believe in Josh Downs as a talent. He's an excellent route-runner and a separation specialist, and in an offense with a capable, accurate quarterback and a smart, high-volume offensive scheme, he might be a fantasy WR1. Unfortunately, as we saw in London last Sunday, the Colts' passing game is a mess. Daniel Jones has the league's sixth-lowest passer rating and third-lowest EPA per dropback (ahead of only Baker Mayfield and Jameis Winston) and has been pressured 60 times through four games, sixth-most for any quarterback. He's thrown for fewer than 170 yards twice and does not have multiple touchdown passes in a single game this season ... but does have an interception in every game.

In ideal circumstances with Keenan Allen inactive (and Alec Pierce still on IR) against the Commanders defense, Downs had just three catches on four targets for 16 yards last Sunday. The leading receiver on the team was Laquon Treadwell, with just 42 yards, and Jones finished with just 143 passing yards and no TDs against a team that had previously allowed 291.7 yards per game and 11 touchdowns in three games. Allen is likely to return this week and the Steelers' pass defense has been far more effective than Washington's. Until proven otherwise, there's simply no ceiling for Downs in this offense and the floor is fewer than five fantasy points (which has happened twice).

What to do ❓ Considering how good he looked in Weeks 2 and 3, Downs isn't a must-sit like Sutton, as he could have another okay day purely on volume — think six catches for 70 yards and exactly 10 fantasy points. But if that's as good as you're going to get, there are a number of better WR3 or FLEX plays.

Dalton Kincaid, TE, Bills at Rams

Joe Brady and the Bills have some explaining to do with regard to Dalton Kincaid, and we actually saw him try after the Patriots game. What do I mean? Well, over the first two weeks, Kincaid had a 25% target share and 30% air yards share in Buffalo and was averaging a position-high 4.7 yards per route run. He looked legitimately elite and was featured in my Week 2 Stock Report here at Yahoo. In the two weeks since? Kincaid's dropped to a 9% target share, 11% air yards share and just 1.2 yards per route run.

This has always seemed to happen with Kincaid over the years in Buffalo — his production is excellent, even elite, but his usage and offensive role never seem to consistently reflect that. And unfortunately, it's hard to see him bouncing back in a matchup with the Rams. Los Angeles has allowed a league-low 85 receiving yards to tight ends through one month.

Not 85 yards per game ... 85 yards total.

They're No. 1 against the position in yards per target (2.9) and have not allowed a single explosive catch to tight ends all year. For fantasy, they're allowing just 5.13 points per game to the position and held both Isaiah Likely and George Kittle (albeit in Week 1) to fewer than eight fantasy points. I really like Kincaid as a fantasy asset and sincerely hope Brady and Co. utilize him correctly rest-of-season ... but I'm fading him for one more week with this defense on the docket.

What to do ❓ Tight end is a shallow position, and Kincaid really is that good, so even with everything I've said above, he's a fringe TE1. But he's certainly not the top-five play he was after the first couple of weeks, and you should absolutely play Likely, Colston Loveland, Juwan Johnson and Tucker Kraft over him and could consider streamers like Mike Gesicki and T.J. Hockenson as well.
