item.title: Why the 49ers likely won’t shadow Jaxon Smith Njigba
item.description: The 49ers aren’t likely to put Deommodore Lenoir on Seattle’s star receiver.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers have quite the challenge ahead of them this week, as they’ll have to find a way to cover Seattle Seahawks star receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who is off to a torrid pace this season with 32 catches for 481 yards and six touchdowns through four games.

Regardless of quarterback, Smith-Njigba has produced, and the 49ers will have to find a way to mitigate the defense. Interestingly, they’ve been among the league’s best though at limiting explosives, which is exactly what the Seahawks will try to accomplish when funneling passes to their star receiver.

In years past, when Charvarius Ward was on the team, he could be a corner that the 49ers used to shadow elite outside receivers. Deommodore Lenoir has asked for that assignment as well. But San Francisco has elected not to do so.

Why has that been the case, and why will that likely continue on Sunday?

“There’s always things you can do and that’s always something that’s definitely within the system. But, those guys nowadays are a little bit different,” defensive coordinator Raheem Morris said when asked on Thursday. “Back in the day when you shadowed somebody, you moved, the other people didn’t move. That was back when Marvin Harrison played on one side and Reggie Wayne played on one side and they just sat there. But as you see in today’s game, there’s a bunch of different things that happen, moving parts. People move, they move inside, they move outside, they move into the backfield, particularly these guys and how they game plan. That’s not always the best thing for the team at times.

“[Lenoir] will be matched up with [Smith-Njigba] a bunch. He will match up a little bit. They cannot stay away from each other, but we won’t do necessarily the shadow thing where you follow him inside, you follow him outside. There’s things we have to do, how we play our game, that won’t be able to pinpoint that all the time, but there will definitely be moments that they’ll get a chance to get together. I don’t know if that’s a nice answer of saying no, but it’s just one of those things of it’s just not the same as it used to be.”

One of Smith-Njigba’s biggest assets is the way he wins regardless of placement on the field, and the Seahawks do a good job drawing him targets by aligning him all over the place. That’s a key reason why the 49ers can’t regularly assign a corner to shadow.

“It’s a bunch of different things [why shadowing isn’t ideal],” Morris continued. “You have these corners, whether it be Patrick Surtain or whether it was Jalen Ramsey or whether it’s DMo. Those receivers are all over the place. As you see our guys moving around all over the place, there’s not just a stationary X anymore, a stationary Z. It just doesn’t work that way. There’s definitely times you can. There’s definitely got-to-have-it moments you can match those things up. It’s definitely dictated by the call at times like some of those things give things away. These quarterbacks nowadays are too smart to just go out there and determine things and dictate things before the snap. You want to be able to sort it out a little bit as they’re taking the snap, taking their drop, going through their process, if that makes sense.”

The 49ers will have to devise a gameplan to limit the star wideout’s targets, and they’ve done a great job of limiting explosives so far. But Smith-Njigba will be their biggest challenge yet, and the 49ers will also be on the road in a big rivalry game on Sunday.

item.title: The Cowboys’ brand is soul-crushing embarrassment
item.description: So many people are to blame for this mess.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys were awful on Thursday night, and managed to make history in the worst possible way. By losing to the Buccaneers, Dallas became the second team since 1975 to lose to an 0-4 team at home. It’s what we’ve come to expect from the Cowboys’ exceptionalism over the last three decades — because exceptionally mediocre has become their brand.

It would be easier to swallow for fans if there was a singular nexus of blame, something you can easily point to and say, “This is why Dallas is losing.“ Unfortunately, there’s no one answer to what’s gone wrong, no silver bullet, nothing to focus on, correct, and get better. Sure, you can point to Jerry and Stephen Jones as being the problem — and make no mistake, they are problems, but there are so many issues. Dallas has shuffled coaches over the years, made splashy trades, invested huge money in their stars, and yet they’ll still lose to a winless football team with a backup QB under center making his first NFL start.

As mentioned, Jerry and Stephen Jones are huge problems. They’ve been problems for a long time. The platonic ideal of an interfering owner, Jerry has been convinced he’s the smartest man in the room for the better part of four decades. Jones boldly stated that his team was going to get better by subtraction when it came to trading away Micah Parsons — they haven’t. He was a driving force behind trading a first-round pick for DT Quinnen Williams, citing a need to shore up Dallas’ run defense. Williams has been objectively disappointing since his arrival, grading out as a mid-tier starter, not someone you trade the future for. This was a team that had three-straight 12 win seasons under Mike McCarthy, whom Jerry fired because he couldn’t get the Cowboys over the hump — giving the keys to Brian Schottenheimer, a mediocre coach in his own right. Stephen has always been there to cater to his father’s worst tendencies, typified by the trade for Joey Porter Jr. Make no mistake: He’s a phenomenal football player, but it’s the kind of shortsighted deal you make when you’re convinced the team is one player away, not for where Dallas is now.

Brian Schottenheimeris a problem. The Cowboys coach now has a 9-12-1 record, he’s dragged the team down since arriving and has tinkered in a way that has caused demonstrable damage to Dak Prescott’s game. Schottenheimer admitted that he was changing too much with respect to the QB position, which is a wild admission when you have a 10-year pro under center and you’re treating him like a third-year QB who need to be rebuilt. In addition, Schottenheimer didn’t really have answers as to why the clock management was so bad at the end of the Cowboys’ loss to the Ravens in Brazil. It’s become apparent that his hiring was a massive mistake, and that Dallas would be a better team right now if they kept Mike McCarthy, or the promoted Kellen Moore instead of losing him, or hell — if they even kept Jason Garrett at this rate.

It’s not entirely his fault, but Dak Prescott has become a problem too. The one thing that dooms NFL offenses isn’t necessarily bad QB play, but inconsistency. Unfortunately for Prescott, he’s become an incredibly inconsistent quarterback capable of phenomenal highs and also staggering lows. One game he’ll look like an All-Pro worthy of being named a Top 3 QB, then the next he’ll play like he did on Thursday night, struggling against a defense that ranked 21st in pass defense entering Week 5. Dak has become a fairweather QB. If CeeDee Lamb is getting open routinely, and the run game is clicking — then he’ll pick teams apart. Get hit with a little adversity and instead of solving the problem, Prescott will have a tendency to force the ball, try to will something to happen, and put himself in a hole as a result.

Not to be left out, the Dallas defense is also an issue. The belief was that hiring Christian Parker away from the Eagles would allow this team to emulate Philadelphia’s defensive success, but instead it’s been a mess. Despite having solid talent on that side of the ball, the defense is ranking near the league’s worst in every single statistical category. The Cowboys are 24th against the pass, 30th against the run, 28th in points allowed — and 30th in overall defense. When you have a porous defense it plays into the worst traits of this Dallas offense, putting the team in a hole and asking Dak to throw his way out of it — which is what leads to so many uneccesary turnovers.

Oh, and special teams allowed blocked field goals in back-to-back games, just for good measure.

The worst part about all this for Cowboys fans is that there’s no easy way out. There isn’t a light at the end of the tunnel. It might take time to fix if this was simply a coaching problem, a QB problem, or defensive issues — but everything flows out of the Joneses at the top. Neither Jerry, nor Stephen are going away, and their unbelievable knack for making horrible decisions is indicative of most things when billionaires get involved. The Cowboys are a mess once more, mediocrity is their brand, and there’s no escape.

item.title: Talking about the Browns’ 3-1 start: Team’s new identity setting the stage
item.description: The Cleveland Browns positive start can be attributed to Todd Monken’s team identity. Now, can it sustain?
item.content:encoded:
Every season, the NFL has a team that surprises everyone and comes out of nowhere in a positive way. It’s fair to say that the NFL has three of those teams this season, two in the AFC and one in the NFC. The Cleveland Browns and the Las Vegas Raiders are a combined 6-1 to start the season, while the New York Giants are 3-1 in an NFC East that contains the Dallas Cowboys and the Philadelphia Eagles.

Out of all the teams that are 3-1, the Browns being 3-1 are the biggest surprise. The question that everyone wants to know is whether the 3-1 start is a sign that things are changing or is it a mirage.

It wasn’t long ago Cleveland had the same 3-1 record. Just a few years ago in 2021. However, that team didn’t make the playoffs. In the 2023 season, the Browns had a surprising start and that team found a way to make the playoffs despite injuries derailing them.

Fast forward to now, Cleveland is back at 3-1. It’s fair to say after their Week 1 performance against the Jacksonville Jaguars, many people were writing the Browns off. Four weeks in, the narrative around the team has changed, but why (besides winning)?

It’s not as cut and dry, but HC Todd Monken’s group has started to slowly find their identity as a team. Identity comes at different times for teams; the earlier the better, especially with a new head coach. It’s fair to say that the Browns have discovered their identity early, and it’s starting to materialize as a physical, gritty team that will turn every game into a phone booth type of battle. Thursday night’s game against the Pittsburgh Steelers showcased that identity. The score isn’t indicative of how the game went. The Browns physically manhandled the Steelers for the majority of the time. Cleveland looked faster, more physical, and had more energy throughout the entire game.

On the offensive side of the ball, the numbers don’t look appealing, but it’s a unit that is slowly starting to find cohesion. The offensive line appears to be much improved from a year ago, the skill position group has received a facelift, and the quarterback play has the stability game-to-game (not within each game) that the team has lacked.

Defensively, the unit doesn’t have an alpha star anymore, but they have retained their identity and principles which made them great last season.

With belief comes some doubt, and of course there are reasons to doubt if this 3-1 start by the Browns is actually legitimate, with many people waiting for the shoe to drop. It’s fair to believe no one is buying the Browns’ 3-1 start due to the opponents they played:

  • Week 2: Tampa Bay Buccaneers (team is unraveling, then found a victory on Thursday Night Football)
  • Week 3: Carolina Panthers (team might actually be good, but injuries have been overwhelming)
  • Week 4: Pittsburgh Steelers (division rival)

All three of the games that Cleveland won, they weren’t favored to win. As much as people question if the Browns are legitimate, the question can be asked for the Las Vegas Raiders as well:

  • Week 1: Miami Dolphins (could be the worst team in the league)
  • Week 2: Los Angeles Chargers (one of the biggest disappointments of the year)
  • Week 3: New Orleans Saints (might be overrated)
  • Week 4: Kansas City Chiefs (best team in division, but Raiders gave them run for their money)

It’s hard to imagine this Cleveland team falling off completely. In fact, this team could be getting better. Peaking early in the season isn’t necessarily a good thing because you tend to burn out later as the season goes on, but the Browns have yet to play a complete game.

The offense will continue to get better, the offensive line will continue to have cohesion, and the quarterback play will improve week to week. The same can be said for the defense in terms of their play. The team doesn’t have the high-end talent to make a deep playoff run, but Cleveland has the talent to give teams problems. The Browns haven’t arrived yet as a true contender, but teams shouldn’t take this team lightly.

Legit or mirage? Is Monken’s team identity established already? How do you view the 3-1 start?

item.title: ‘Dominant force’ Maxx Crosby the latest test for Patriots O-line
item.description: The Raiders star had one of his best games of 2025 against the Patriots.
item.content:encoded:
Had the offseason gone as planned, the New England Patriots would not be going up against Maxx Crosby this Sunday. Instead, the Las Vegas Raiders star would be playing for the Baltimore Ravens this weekend.

However, Baltimore famously backed out of the deal after Crosby failed his physical, retaining two first-round draft picks while seeing the 29-year-old go back to Las Vegas. Seven months later, he continues to play his typical high-volume role along the Raiders edge as if nothing had happened.

For the Patriots, that is not exactly good news. Crosby, after all, continues to be a problem for opposing offensive lines.

“It’s a guy that you have to pay attention to until the whistle blows, and a little bit after,” said starting right tackle Morgan Moses. “He’s always around. He’s a max-effort guy, that’s what he does. It’s hats off to him, what he’s been able to do in his career in this league so far. He’s a dominant force so we have to be able to have our details, our technique and our fundamentals, and know where he’s at all the time, and obviously limit him to the ball.”

Through four games this season, Crosby and the Raiders defense have been among the most disruptive forces in football. The team as a whole ranks second in the NFL in quarterback pressure rate (35.6%), with Crosby checking in at No. 4 with 25 total pressures including a pair of sacks. He also forced fumble and registered a recovery.

Long story short, he is looking every bit the player he has in the past — including last year, when he had a sack and season-best seven total disruptions in a 20-13 Raiders win in Foxborough. Naturally, the Patriots know the importance of slowing him down.

“He’s a great player. We have to try our best to stop him,” said running back TreVeyon Henderson. “We know it’s not going to be easy, so we all have to help each other out to do a good job stopping him.”

Based on alignment charting, that job will mostly fall on Moses and the right side of New England’s line. Crosby has lined up there for 176 of his 222 defensive snaps this season (79.3%).

However, as Mike Vrabel pointed out, the Patriots need to be on high-alert at all times.

“Maxx will go wherever he wants to go, and he will do whatever he wants to do, and it’s worked out really, really well,” the Patriots’ head coach said. “I have a lot of respect for Maxx Crosby as a person and also as a player. So, we’ll have to know where he is on every single play.”

Vrabel in general has been impressed with Las Vegas’ ability to force offenses into mistakes under a first-year coaching staff led by Klint Kubiak and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard.

“Guys have come from different places, and they’ve really put together a cohesive group,” he said. “[Adam] Butler was there, [Jeremy] Chinn was there, Maxx was there, [Malcolm] Koonce was there. But they’ve been able to supplement that with the guys off the football with [Nakobe] Dean and [Quay] Walker, and obviously continue to add guys inside, and then also [Kwity] Paye. So, they’ve really come together and gelled well together, and we will have to know where Maxx is, certainly, to start every play.”

item.title: Raiders News: Ashton Jeanty was limited at practice on Thursday
item.description: The Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty appeared on the injury report with a new injury
item.content:encoded:
The Las Vegas Raiders are getting ready to face off against the New England Patriots. They hope to bounce back from the heartbreaking loss to the Kansas City Chiefs.

The team has been struggling in the running game. Ashton Jeanty has not been fully healthy since his summer injury, and it is showing on the field. As the injury lingers, Jeanty has remained a full participant in practice. That changed on Thursday, when he went from full to a limited designation for practice. However, this time it wasn’t the ankle; it was a foot injury.

The Raiders’ depth at running back, if he can’t go, is a strong point, with Mike Washington Jr. as a backup. It would also give Dylan Laube a shot at more playing time. It might be the time to rest Jeanty and allow the ankle to fully heal. Jeanty needs to be healthy by the end of the year when it is time to push for the playoffs.

item.title: Our offense vs. their defense: Minnesota Vikings
item.description: The Saints’ offense has a tall task against one of the league’s premiere defenses.
item.content:encoded:
After the first month of NFL football, the New Orleans Saints hold one of the best offenses in the league. Despite their 1-3 record, New Orleans has had a premier offense across the league, but will face the NFL’s best defensive play-caller, Brian Flores.

After four weeks, the Saints are tied with the 10th-best scoring offense, averaging 26.3 points per game. The Vikings defense, on the other hand, has allowed the fewest points, allowing just 12.8 points per game to opposing offenses.

It’s no doubt this is the week New Orleans tries to establish the run, holding the sixth-worst rushing offense in the league and averaging just 88.5 rushing yards per game. Minnesota’s defense is known for its exotic pass-rushing looks, blitzing the quarterback over 70% of the time. Establishing the run will force the Vikings to ease up on the pass rush, but so far this season, teams haven’t found success in the run game. Minnesota has the seventh-best run defense in the NFL, allowing just 94.5 rushing yards per game.

But it’s likely New Orleans won’t find success in the run game. Running back Travis Etienne Jr. is on the injured reserve after suffering a hamstring injury, and Alvin Kamara was a non-participant in Wednesday’s walk-through with a back injury. With these injuries, the Saints are likely to lean on their passing offense, which ranks as one of the best in the NFL. New Orleans is averaging 278.5 passing yards per game, which ranks fourth in the league.

Quarterback Tyler Shough is set to face the most fierce pass rush he has so far this season, even despite the brutal loss to the Atlanta Falcons. Shough is currently third in the NFL in passing yards with 1,203 and tied second in touchdowns. He’ll likely lean on his WR1, Chris Olave, who is second in the NFL in receiving yards with 491.

The Saints are in desperate need of getting back to winning games, but facing this Minnesota defense may be their hardest task so far this season. Over the last three weeks of the season, the Vikings are allowing opposing offenses to score just 9.6 points per game, and aren’t looking to budge against a New Orleans offense that starts slow week in and week out.

But while this is the best defense the Saints will see so far this season, the opposite is true for the Vikings. They haven’t seen an offense as successful as New Orleans this season. While they did face the Chicago Bears in Week 2, it wasn’t without heavy rain and an eventual injury to quarterback Caleb Williams. Will the Saints find a way to get back on track against the 4-0 Vikings and their fierce defense?

item.title: 3 things that must improve about the Chiefs after the bye week
item.description: What are the areas of the game Kansas City needs to work on after four weeks?
item.content:encoded:
There’s reason to feel confident the Kansas City Chiefs can build on their 4-0 start and return to postseason glory. They’ve had a strong start to the season, but the team needs to address a few areas over the bye week to stay atop the AFC standings.

Here are the three things the Chiefs most need to improve on for the rest of the campaign:

1. Third-down defense

This season, the Chiefs allow 37% of third-down conversions, ranking 13th in the NFL.

The Chiefs’ pressure rate is middle of the pack (24%), but on third down, they rank 25th (40%). The team has only one third-down sack this year: defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah’s strip sack of Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix in Week 1.

The pass rush is the clearest path to getting off the field more often. Defensive tackle Chris Jones needs to be more disruptive on pass downs, because defensive ends George Karlaftis and rookie R Mason Thomas seem to be muddying the pocket from the edge at a good rate.

2. True pass protection

The Chiefs’ offense has operated well by leaning on the run game and its effect on the defense with play action from under center. It’s been refreshing to see, but Kansas City still needs to give quarterback Patrick Mahomes time to operate on straight dropbacks.

So far this season, the pass blocking has been subpar in true pass sets. Rookie left tackle Kahlil Benson has allowed six pressures (three quarterback hits) over 48 true pass sets, according to Pro Football Focus. That means the Chiefs drop back into a traditional pass play an average of only 12 times per game.

As opponents get tougher, Mahomes will need to win games by throwing the ball when the defense knows he is. The return of left tackle Josh Simmons (back) — regardless of how the right tackle position is handled — feels like the only path to significant improvement here.

3. Playmaking from pass catchers

We probably aren’t making a big enough deal of wide receiver Tyquan Thornton likely missing the entire regular season with a dislocated ankle. He’s been the pass-catching group’s biggest playmaker so far, but that says little given how well this team’s pass offense has performed this year.

Whether the run game opens it up or Mahomes puts passes on the money, the receivers haven’t been asked to do much more than execute the play so far this year. Without Thornton (and No. 1 target Rashee Rice (hamstring) in the short term, potentially), the offense desperately needs receivers like Xavier Worthy, Jalen Royals and rookie Cyrus Allen to step up and make plays themselves.

Whether it’s Royals’ run-after-catch ability or Allen’s route running, the offense needs to use these players to their strengths while Worthy likely sees an increase in overall target share. The former first-round pick needs to look the part moving forward.

That said, the pass-catching group’s playmaking may be impossible to elevate without a trade or free-agent signing. The NFL trade deadline is November 10, between Weeks 9 and 10 of the season. Look for general manager Brett Veach to make a move as he has in previous years, whether it was wide receiver Kadarius Toney in 2022 or DeAndre Hopkins in 2024.

item.title: Seahawks vs. 49ers, Week 5 preview: The keys to Seattle giving the 49ers their first loss
item.description: Seattle must close the gaps, pressure Brock Purdy and stay disciplined to hand San Francisco its first loss.
item.content:encoded:
The 3-1 Seattle Seahawks head into Sunday looking to hand the 4-0 San Francisco 49ers their first loss of the season. San Francisco has looked like one of the league’s best teams through the first month, while Seattle has started to establish an identity built around an aggressive defense and an offense that has shown flashes of efficiency.

This is an important game for Seattle beyond the standings. A win would prevent the 49ers from creating early separation in the division, give the Seahawks a head-to-head advantage and provide a significant boost heading into a more difficult portion of the schedule. Seattle has already beaten the Patriots and Cardinals, lost to Washington and handled an 0-4 Chargers team in Week 4. Beating San Francisco would be a different kind of statement.

Close the cracks in the run defense

Seattle’s run defense remains one of the biggest areas to watch, and the tape shows a potential weakness opponents can attack: the space between the interior defensive linemen and the edges.

That is exactly the kind of space Kyle Shanahan wants to create.

Outside zone remains the foundation of San Francisco’s rushing attack, and Christian McCaffrey is playing at an extremely high level. Through four games, McCaffrey has carried the ball 50 times for 218 yards and four touchdowns while adding 16 catches for 122 yards.

The important part for Seattle isn’t simply stopping McCaffrey at the line of scrimmage. It is preventing him from turning small creases into five-, eight- or 15-yard gains.

When the 49ers can consistently run the football, Shanahan gets to open up the entire playbook. Motion becomes more dangerous. Play-action becomes more convincing. The defense has to hesitate before attacking the quarterback.

And that is where San Francisco can really hurt Seattle.

Shanahan will also have to adjust without Kyle Juszczyk, whose injury removes one of the most versatile pieces of the 49ers’ formation and motion game. Juszczyk isn’t just a traditional fullback. San Francisco frequently uses him in pre-snap motion to create leverage and manipulate defensive assignments before the snap.

The concept is simple but difficult to defend: Juszczyk can move across the formation before the snap, forcing the defense to communicate and adjust, then enter the play with momentum as a blocker. Instead of identifying where the defense is lined up, the motion can create a better blocking angle and put an extra body into the run fit.

Shanahan has been doing this for years, so losing Juszczyk won’t suddenly make the concept disappear. The 49ers will find other ways to recreate it.

Seattle has to make those adjustments matter.

Pressure Brock Purdy and finish the play

One of the biggest lessons from Seattle’s previous games is that pressure alone isn’t enough.

Marcus Mariota showed how quickly a quarterback can neutralize the pass rush when he consistently gets the ball out on time. Washington’s quick passing game limited Seattle’s opportunities to get home, even though the Seahawks were able to generate pressure.

San Francisco can use the same blueprint.

Brock Purdy is also much more dangerous once a play breaks down. He has the ability to escape the pocket, extend plays and pick up yards with his legs. Through four games, Purdy has already rushed 20 times for 122 yards and a touchdown.

Seattle has already seen quarterbacks hurt its defense with their legs this season. Drake Maye rushed seven times for 47 yards in Week 1, while Justin Herbert ran six times for 40 yards in Week 4.

The Seahawks cannot allow Purdy to turn third-and-long into a scramble drill. More importantly, pressure has to become sacks.

Hits are nice. Hurries are useful. But against an offense as efficient as San Francisco’s, allowing Purdy to escape pressure and still complete the play is almost as damaging as not pressuring him at all.

Seattle needs to collapse the pocket, maintain rush-lane discipline and finish.

The challenge is tough once 49ers dit not allow a sack yet.

Don’t let Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel, and George Kittle dictate the game

San Francisco’s receiving corps has added another dimension with Mike Evans.

Evans gives Purdy a legitimate back-shoulder and contested-catch option, particularly in situations where the quarterback needs a reliable safety valve outside the numbers. Through four games, Evans has 17 receptions for 213 yards and two touchdowns.

That creates an interesting matchup for Seattle’s secondary, especially if Evans is consistently targeted against smaller defensive backs. Josh Jobe could see some of those snaps, and the size difference is something San Francisco can attempt to exploit. Maybe Trevon Diggs can be elevated again, especially as Nehemiah Pritchett seems to be dealing with an injury.

Then there is Deebo Samuel.

This version of Deebo looks much closer to the player San Francisco originally fell in love with than the version we have seen at times in recent seasons. Through four games, Samuel has 14 receptions for 185 yards and three touchdowns while also rushing seven times for 74 yards.

That versatility changes the math for the defense.

Deebo can line up outside, move into the slot, take a handoff, catch a screen and turn a routine touch into a chunk play. Seattle’s tackling discipline will be critical because the first defender often isn’t the one who ends the play.

And then there is George Kittle. Fresh off an Achilles injury, Kittle has 16 catches for 244 yards and four touchdowns through four games, averaging more than 15 yards per reception.

His impact isn’t limited to the passing game. Kittle’s ability as a blocker gives Shanahan another way to manipulate the front, especially when Seattle is trying to defend outside-zone concepts.

Seattle cannot allow Kittle to become both a sixth offensive lineman and a vertical receiving threat on the same afternoon.

There is no room for mistakes

If there is one thing Seattle cannot repeat from the Chargers game, it is the penalty problem.

Seattle committed 14 penalties for 150 yards against Los Angeles, and the Chargers committed 16 penalties for 130 yards. What should have been a comfortable Seattle victory became a game that remained alive until the final drive.

That cannot happen against San Francisco. The 49ers are too efficient, and their offense is too good at turning extended drives into points. Giving Shanahan free first downs or putting the defense in disadvantageous situations is an invitation to disaster.

Turnovers are another obvious concern. Seattle has already seen how costly they can be after the loss to Washington. Sam Darnold also struggled against the Chargers, throwing for 168 yards with two touchdowns and an interception.

Against the 49ers, a three-turnover game probably isn’t survivable.

Seattle doesn’t need Darnold to throw for 350 yards. It needs him to protect the football, take the throws that are there and avoid giving San Francisco short fields. The margin for error is going to be small.

Brian Fleury needs to make the run game show up

This might be the most important offensive question for Seattle.

Brian Fleury has done a good job getting the passing game moving, but the Seahawks still haven’t found that consistent rhythm on the ground that can make the entire offense more difficult to defend.

Through four games, Seattle has rushed for 441 yards at 3.9 yards per carry.

The 49ers, meanwhile, have already shown that their defense can be vulnerable to teams willing to run directly at them and attack the edges.

That is the good news.

The bad news is that Seattle’s offensive line has struggled to consistently create movement at the line of scrimmage on physical runs. That’s where the game plan has to matter.

Duo runs and concepts that attack the edges could give Seattle opportunities, but the Seahawks cannot simply call the plays and hope the blocks develop. The offensive line has to win its individual matchups, the backs have to hit the correct gaps and the play design has to give them a chance.

Seattle cannot win this game asking Darnold to carry the offense with his arm. The Seahawks need a credible rushing threat, even if that means grinding out four yards at a time.

If Fleury can get the run game moving, everything else becomes easier. Play-action becomes more effective. Protection improves. Darnold gets cleaner reads. And San Francisco’s defense has to respect more than just the passing game.

That is the version of Seattle’s offense that has the best chance of keeping pace.

Third down is where this game could be decided

One trend worth watching is how aggressively defenses have attacked Seattle on third down.

The Seahawks’ offensive line has been inconsistent at times, and some of Seattle’s concepts take too long to develop against pressure. When opponents blitz, the answer can’t always be a route combination that requires Darnold to hold the ball and wait for something to open.

The Seahawks need answers built into the play call.

Quick-game concepts, hot routes and throws designed to punish pressure can force San Francisco to think twice before sending extra rushers. But those answers only work if Seattle is consistently creating manageable third downs.

That brings the entire game plan back to the run game. If Seattle can stay ahead of the sticks, Fleury has a much larger menu of options. If the Seahawks are constantly facing third-and-8 or third-and-10, San Francisco can unleash its pressure packages and dictate the terms.

That’s exactly what Seattle has to avoid.

Final thoughts

This game will be decided by the details, but those details are connected. If San Francisco is consistently running the ball, Shanahan can use motion and play-action to create hesitation. If Purdy gets clean escape lanes, the pass rush loses some of its value. If Evans, Deebo and Kittle are winning consistently, the 49ers can force Seattle’s defense into uncomfortable personnel and coverage decisions. And if the Seahawks commit penalties or turn the ball over, San Francisco is good enough to turn those mistakes into points.

But Seattle has a path to making this game uncomfortable for the 49ers, too. Close the gaps in the run defense, force Purdy to operate from a collapsing pocket and finish pressures with sacks. On offense, find a way to generate enough movement in the run game to keep San Francisco honest, protect Darnold and punish the blitz. The Seahawks don’t need a flawless performance. They need a disciplined one. If they can eliminate the self-inflicted mistakes and make San Francisco win every inch, Seattle has a legitimate chance to hand the 49ers their first loss of the season — and send a much louder message about where this Seahawks team belongs in the NFC West.
